item.title: Wine walks
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
For the last two years I've participated in annual events where a group of people can walk around the vineyars and sample the produce of local wine makers. Yesterday I was lucky eniugh to participate in the Muscadet walk, in the small village of Saint Fiacre , near the "Capital" of Muscadet, Vallet, in France.

Muscadet is a dry white wine associated with seafood, fish and as a drink that could be mixed with sweeter syrups (either alcoholic or not) and made into a cocktail called 'Kir'

About Muscadet: It's had a bad press, being seen as a low quality Muscadet and most folks don't understand that there are many different types of Muscadet wines. They are all made from the "Melon de Bourgogne "grape variety, BUT the terroir and the slopes all change what kind of muscadet you'll get, plus the vinification process.

It was a chilly Sunday morning as we set off, the first fingers of autumn draped over the fields, but soon the sun's warmth came and as we walked jumpers and coats were quickly shed. Until the first stop, people chatted away about their days, and their jobs and lives. We came to the first producer, and were welcomed with a wonderful band playing lively music . Jazz and some typical French songs. The first wine was an amazing muscadet that surprised and delighted. A nibble and on we went. The sun claimed up and a hot day burnet the clouds away. We hugged the edges of the fields.or the shade, drinking water to stave off any cramp. We tasted a different wine at every stop, after about 2 or 3 kilometres.

item.title: Depth and times
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Chaos is a generative order. Chaos created.

It isn't the everyday measures or judgement, but a deeper ,contrasting force.

We cannot explain away the force from chaos, or its generative nature. Chaos cannot control.

Spirit is an image formed from the choas, like the mandlebrot set fractals created from the depths of choas.

The spirit of the times is not the supreme meaning

Intuition hit us and we should ask: How could I know.

The spirit of the times cannot see the chaos of the depths

We can lose our MEASURE

And miss the reality. By searching to KNOW, to measure all, we lose the essence

Knowledge is not judgement or measure

The melting of the spirit of the times with the spirit of the depths

If you start paying attention you become whole

The self and the ego need to be connected

the depths communicated with images and stmbols, not words

this is where architypes come from this is why politicians try so hard to be archytypes but we need to be aware of this

the depths provide mercy

The depths contain everything in you, what is. All

The way of what is to come

What is is not what you think is or even what you perceive to be

Using non human methods to discover is a way around the judgement

Children construct an ego to protect them froom the waves of the self and then you have to deconstruct that to find it again

Follow your own way in your own self

The spirit of the times changed when knoledge and certanty were broken in world war 2

Today we now argue with fake news; We cast doub on what is

i found the animus

the psyche is alive

the introversion of the libido

We search for the hollow things of this world as we try to escape the depths and the self

without a dance with your soul you will be driven by your desires

dreams are the voice of your soul

separate the body from the moind

reunite them

reconnect them

your ego (will) must drive the process. strength, courage, humility and patience

Introversion and this means a journey inside

meditation and active imagination

item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Beautés aux perspectives cachées
Peu évidentes, mais quotidiennes,
Persistantes et perspicaces,
Choisies, observées, transformées.

Les coins ombragés, acceptés,
Ignorés par les passants.
Vestigium pedis,
La beauté du Maître.
Ces toiles d’araignée imprégnées
De la rosée du matin.

Les sentiers battus et leurs alignements,
Plantes oubliées, négligées,
Déchets jetés,
Graines de pissenlit soufflées au vent.
Les brouillards d’urine de chiens et de déjections de chats,
Les spirales laissées par les vers
Marquent le voyage :
Tous vers une même destination,
En compagnies différentes

Voici une traduction en français, fidèle au sens, au ton et aux références, en conservant les ruptures, titres et respirations du poème. J’ai privilégié une langue poétique plutôt que littérale quand c’était nécessaire.


---

L’œil du regardeur

L’œil du regardeur

Y a-t-il de la beauté dans ces arrière-ruelles ?
Ces zones poussiéreuses jonchées de débris ?
Des orties à demi drapées sur des tas d’ordures,
Mégots et préservatifs abandonnés.
Au fond de ces chemins boueux, de ces passages murés de briques,
Sous des ciels d’ardoise, impitoyables ?

L’ÉTREINTE DE L’HIVER

Y a-t-il de la beauté dans ces paquets de chips froissés ?
Dans les tortillons de vers et les crottes de chien ?
Y a-t-il de la joie dans ces pissenlits à demi fanés,
Leurs graines soufflées par le vent humide des pots d’échappement ?
Des brumes de mégots murmurent en s’élevant,
Ces herbes folles qui osent ces coins humides ?
Ces cages d’escalier crasseuses où jouaient les enfants ?

JOIE

La joie des voix d’enfants.

Y a-t-il de l’espoir dans ces paysages
Où la pauvreté broie les os fatigués ?
Des toiles d’araignée serties de rosée,
Des traces de pneus dans des ornières pleines d’eau.
Des portes de garages couvertes de graffitis, entrouvertes,
L’espoir des maisons en rangées, les vitres brisées.

CORVÉE

Y a-t-il une chance dans ces seringues vides ?
Aiguilles sales, douleur vive.
Y a-t-il des messages dans les bombes de peinture ?
Ou dans ces sacs à moitié remplis de colle ?
Y avait-il de l’amour dans ces préservatifs ?
Le va-et-vient rapide contre le mur.
Y avait-il de la beauté dans ces souffles
Exhalés de joints roulés d’avance ?

GONFLÉ

Cette bravade au regard vide,
Haussement d’épaules — « et alors ? » — rejet à deux sous.
Sourire honteux, air de chien battu, sourire écorné,
Qui rampe dans ces arrière-ruelles.
La brume de novembre au petit matin, hantée.

Y a-t-il donc de la beauté dans ces coins poussiéreux,
Oubliés ou abandonnés dans les misères du quotidien,
Dans l’espoir, l’amour ou la beauté ?
Avons-nous besoin de ces routes de campagne,
Leur beauté figée, de carte postale,
Des Dales majestueuses, ouvertes, inspirantes ?

LES DOWNS, LE NORD, LE SUD

Je passerai ma vie dans ces arrière-ruelles.
Elles ne mènent nulle part, mais donnent accès.
Délaissées, sous-utilisées.
Utilité quotidienne, plutôt terne.
Leur beauté brûle à travers les yeux.
Carcasses brûlées dans des voies brûlées.

RELÈVE LA TÊTE

Alors, y a-t-il de la beauté dans ces ruelles ?
Pas de champs de blé ni de ciels pleins de corbeaux.
Pas d’hectares moissonnés ni de coteaux fraîchement labourés.
Pas de pignons nobles ni de salles sacrées.
Pas de collines ondulantes ni de chemins bucoliques.
Pas de miel à l’heure du thé, pas d’horloge à dix heures moins cinq.
À qui étaient ces lilas — à Eliot ou à Brooke ?
Abandonnés ici, dans ces terres vagues.
Bonnes seulement pour les papillons ?

COMPOSITION

Le caddie de supermarché, rouillant lentement,
N’est qu’un touriste d’un autre monde,
Comme une hirondelle migrante exotique,
Ici aujourd’hui, disparue demain.
Chez lui parmi les ronces et le lierre,
Chez lui avec les coléoptères et les puces.
Seuls les écoliers empruntent ces passages,
Ou les chercheurs, ou les malades.
Arrière-ruelles aux feuilles mortes et aux mouches,
Au bout d’un chemin cassé, pierreux.

DÉCOMPOSITION

Il y a de la vie dans cette litière de feuilles,
Comme il y a espoir et joie.
Comme la beauté brille là,
Sur les coquilles des morts et dans les os des vivants.
Jeté, oublié — « ne le dis pas à maman ».
Carapace brillante ou feuille tachetée,
Un sac en papier danse dans le vent.

Bien sûr, nous enterrons les morts ou brûlons le passé,
Sa douleur est trop vive pour nous porter doucement,
Sa folie pleine d’erreurs neuves,
Ses désirs vides, son poing qui tremble.

MOURIR D’ATTENDRE

Assieds-toi près du feu et regarde :
Sa main tremble, mouchetée par l’âge.
Flétri, rétréci, comme une vieille relique
Lancée hors d’une cour qui n’existe plus.
Ses os, ses poutres, usés et ouverts,
On voit la veine du bois,
Le grain, gravé, érodé,
Fané même, presque fini.

Considère Phlébas maintenant,
Regarde sa lassitude.
Pas encore noyé ni mort,
Ces ressources seront recyclées.
Dans les arrière-ruelles de son imagination,
Atome à atome, poussière à poussière.

L’INÉVITABILITÉ DE LA MORT

La mort nous arrache, mais nos coquilles
Gisent dans les ruelles, demeure pour d’autres,
Comme un matelas humide, jeté,
Ou des mégots vissés et lancés dans la haie,
La haie qui borde
Ces routes étirées,
Des arrière-ruelles menant partout.

À MOITIÉ LU, À MOITIÉ COMPRIS

Ces textes à moitié lus, à moitié compris,
À moitié étudiés, vite oubliés.
Des éclats de soleil à travers les nuages,
Occupé comme un scarabée, sage comme un ver.
Déchirés par la mort, à moitié connus, appris par cœur à moitié,
Récités souvent en mots murmurés,
Marmonnés au mur, puis
Premier dehors quand la cloche sonnait.
Souvenirs présents mais jamais compris.
De qui était la meilleure plume,
Quels mots nous faisaient froncer les sourcils, rire ou soupirer,
Comparer le bleu au vert, ou la merde au tout ou rien,
Quelle chanson était la meilleure, la pire, ou rien du tout,
Quand chacun a son mot à dire.

BEAUTÉ BIGARRÉE

La beauté rôde dans ces impasses mortes,
Chuchotant dans les fils à linge,
Flottant comme un fantôme — espérant, gémissant, jurant —
Tenant le passé comme une tête tranchée.
Sous les feuilles froissées, la vie bruisse,
Sous des ciels couverts et des regards assombris.
Donner des coups de pied dans les feuilles mortes, joie de l’enfance,
Comme Pétrone, parti rejoindre la majorité.
Frapper le chemin du savoir,
En cacher la vérité — quelle arrogance.

LE MOIS LE PLUS CRUEL

Frappe à la porte et laisse-moi entrer,
Je ne peux plus porter ce fardeau.
Son poids brûlant
Pèse sur moi.
Le crapaud du travail,
Alors que je rejoins les seconds pauvres,
Pas assez bon pour rejoindre les premiers,
Ni assez sage ni assez patient pour être riche.
Ni cupide — j’ai tout donné,
Et donné, et donné, et donné,
Sans jamais penser à prendre un peu.

Hanté par l’équilibre, par l’inclinaison,
Les moulins ont tourné et se sont écartés.
Comme Walter Mitty, je demeure
Dans le pays du fantasme ou des pelotons d’exécution.
Votre Seigneurie, s’il vous plaît, ne retenez pas
Les récompenses et les prix.
Pour une vie de fées et de duvet !
Donnez-les-moi donc.
Je mentirai sur mon CV
Et serai promu alors !
Je prétendrai à l’intelligence,
Ou à un diplôme de l’université de la Vie.

La maison d’Archer fut celle de Brooke,
De qui la plume était la meilleure — voilà la question.
Lève-toi et prends les choses de la vie.
Émerge de ces flaques,
Allongé dans des ruelles à moitié abandonnées,
Comme un monstre du marais primordial,
Traînant en avant, glissant, éclaboussant,
Fonce, noie, meurs, creuse et drogue-toi.
Ces lilas au parfum puissant ne durent pas longtemps,
Puis brunissent, s’humidifient, montent en graine.
Écrits par des fantômes, signés par d’autres,
Je réclame le prix pour moi-même.

LES VIVANTS-MOURANTS

Froid comme la pierre,
Froid comme une pierre
Qui éclate lentement.
Dans l’ombre des pierres
Nous gisons, les vivants mourants.
Dans l’ombre des pierres,
Réfutant la cruauté d’avril
Par l’ensevelissement des morts,
Dans ces voies oubliées
Qui mènent à on-ne-sait-quand.

Regarder le passé à travers le prisme
De la nostalgie et se demander
Pourquoi ce n’est plus comme avant.
Arraché au filet chronophage,
Des tâches à accomplir,
Écrites, gravées sur le papier,
Martelées dans la pierre.

Les Beatles ont menti :
L’amour pris et l’amour donné ne s’équilibrent pas.
Je me tiens dans le champ
Comme un fou de jumelles,
Photographiant des oiseaux rares
Dont personne ne se soucie.
Comme vouloir posséder l’inpossédable,
Capturer des éclats sur le papier,
Prestige ou pathos
Sur le mur :
« J’ÉTAIS ICI »
Comme tant de pisse de chien,
Lavée par la pluie sans fin,
Marquant un territoire perdu depuis longtemps,
Abandonné, puis effacé de l’histoire,
Moqué et renié.

L’argent est la seule chose
Qui ne sera pas possédée :
Transmise, oui, donnée ou empruntée,
Comme une mauvaise nouvelle par un jour d’hiver.

SOIXANTE-DIX ANS

Entre, numéro neuf, ton temps est écoulé.

LE REGARD DE LA BEAUTÉ

Y a-t-il de la beauté dans ces tas de déchets,
Dans les terrils du Nord,
Dans les tours de refroidissement gelées ?
Les voies ferrées et les usines ?
Le jadis grand OZYMANDIAS :
« Regardez mes œuvres et désespérez ».



Y a-t-il donc de la beauté dans des lacets,
Ou des poubelles vides, ou des bouts de ficelle ?
Ou bien les crumpets près du feu
Rougeoient-ils, profonds, chargés de péché ?
Ce chien aux yeux noirs
Qui tire sur mon cœur.
Écrire des poèmes
Que personne ne lit
Ni ne remarque.
Auto-obsédé,
Oublié et interdit.

Y a-t-il de la beauté dans les plumes, dans la fourrure,
Dans les rêveries au museau mouillé ?
Dans la fuite hors du réel, à l’intérieur de nos têtes ?
Est-ce si mal, alors, d’emprunter les chemins de Mitty,
À la recherche d’une grandeur introuvable ?

Sur le pont trop court pour les vivants,
Ces voies amères.
Sont-ce les mêmes arrière-ruelles ?
Ah, nous ne sommes que des épis de blé dans le vent,
Courbés, brisés, fauchés et semés.
Le sang riche de la vie,
Gaspillé dans ce qui aurait pu être.

Il y a plus qu’à coller,
tac, tac, tac.
Après, on mange.

item.title: h1>Connection Before Content: The Three Pillars of Transformative Learning</h1
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded: <h1>Connection Before Content: The Three Pillars of Transformative Learning</h1> <p> For learning to be truly effective, there must first be a genuine connection with the teacher. Our school memories rarely revolve around worksheets or exams; they are about the teachers who inspired us, encouraged us, or cared enough to build a relationship. We remember the feeling of being seen far more than any piece of information we memorised. </p> <blockquote> <p><strong>“You have to love the students.” — Dr John Kingston, Polytech Nantes</strong></p> </blockquote> <p> A healthy, secure rapport is not a bonus in education — it is the prerequisite. When learners feel safe, respected, and recognised, they open up. They participate. They allow curiosity to happen. Without connection, even the best content falls flat. </p> <p> Some students can thrive independently, of course. But most learners need what all humans need: relationship, belonging, and attention. </p> <hr/> <h2>Learning Begins Before School</h2> <p> Think back to childhood. Long before we entered a classroom, we learned to speak, walk (if able), play, interact socially, and navigate the world — all without professional educators. Parents and carers taught us these things through affection, consistency, and presence. </p> <p> <strong>Connection mattered more than content.</strong><br/> The relationship was the curriculum. </p> <p> When children lack connection — when they are ignored, abandoned, or mistreated — their ability to learn is deeply compromised. No amount of curriculum can compensate for the absence of care. </p> <h3>A Painful Illustration: The Case of Genie</h3> <p> Genie’s story is a heartbreaking example of what happens when a child is deprived not only of language, but of love, interaction, and human presence. Genie did not fail to learn because of a lack of intelligence; she was denied the relational environment that makes learning possible. </p> <p> Her case reminds us that connection is not a luxury — it is the scaffolding upon which language, cognition, identity, and trust are built. Without it, even the strongest potential struggles to emerge. </p> <hr/> <h2>The Three Pillars of Transformative Learning</h2> <p> To understand how learning truly unfolds, we can turn to three interconnected pillars: <strong>Connection, Construction, and Conversation.</strong> Together, they guide learners from feeling safe, to feeling motivated, to feeling curious. </p> <h3>1. Connection — Building a Link with Love</h3> <p> Connection is the gateway to learning. When learners feel valued, they risk engagement; when they feel unimportant or judged, they shut down. </p> <ul> <li>Seeing the learner before the lesson</li> <li>Creating trust and emotional safety</li> <li>Offering warmth alongside structure</li> <li>Caring enough to challenge and support</li> </ul> <p><strong>A connected learner is a receptive learner.</strong></p> <h3>2. Construction — Building the Desire to Learn</h3> <p> Once there is connection, teachers can construct the internal motivation that drives active learning. This is where purpose and curiosity begin to grow. </p> <ul> <li>Making learning relevant</li> <li>Building confidence and capability</li> <li>Strengthening autonomy</li> <li>Helping learners feel ownership</li> </ul> <p>When learners <em>want</em> to learn, teaching becomes guidance, not struggle.</p> <h3>3. Conversation — Building the Curiosity to Question</h3> <p> Conversation is where learning becomes transformative. Students shift from passive receivers to active co-creators of knowledge. </p> <ul> <li>Treating learning as dialogue</li> <li>Encouraging questions</li> <li>Nurturing imagination and inquiry</li> <li>Sharing meaning rather than delivering information</li> </ul> <p>Curiosity thrives in dialogue.</p> <hr/> <h2>We Need a Different Way</h2> <p> We cannot continue with a system that breaks both learners <em>and</em> teachers — and then blames them for the fractures. When students feel unseen and teachers are overwhelmed, no amount of curriculum reform will fix the deeper issue. </p> <p> This is not a failure of individuals. It is a failure of a framework that ignores the human foundations of learning: belonging, attention, and trust. </p> <p> If education does not place connection at its centre, we will continue to produce burnout, boredom, and the belief that school is something to survive rather than a place to grow. </p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Connection is not optional. It is the foundation of all meaningful learning.</strong></p> </blockquote>

item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
He saw them clearly:
pelt‑clad figures crouched around dancing tongues of flame, watching the scarlet horizon stretch and disappear.
Stars pinpricked through a velvet sky.
Skeletal trees dissolved into the quicksand of night.Fire was their first teacher.
It taught them how to speak to those near, those far, those alive, those past.
It taught them how to survive.Lionel felt the warmth of those ancient flames as if they still burned beneath his feet.

II. The Hard Road

The island showed him the dangers of travel — the hardships his ancestors endured.He saw children tumbling through leaves, laughing, unaware of how fragile they were.
A broken arm meant death.
A fever meant death.
Loose bowels meant death.
Predators followed the smell of blood.The clan moved constantly, carrying only what they could weave or lift.
Bent‑branch shelters rose and fell with the seasons.
Roots, berries, carrion — whatever the land offered, they took.Lionel felt the weight of their hunger, their fear, their resilience.

III. The Caves of Moving WallsThe island pulled him deeper.Women led the young into hidden caves, stone lamps trembling in their hands.
Light leapt across the walls, making painted animals move — bison lowering their heads, red deer stepping from shadow, handprints blooming and fading.These were the first memory marks, the ancestors of the volcanic island’s mist symbols and spear codes.Lionel felt the echo of those paintings in the mist around him.

IV. The End of IceThe island shifted again.He saw the world warming — ice melting, rivers swelling, seas rising.
Land broke apart.
Families were separated.
Clans became islands.Some islands kept warriors.
Some kept navigators.
Some kept healers.
Some kept builders.But one island — his island — kept memory.The mud pool beneath him hissed louder, as if agreeing.

V. Stone MonumentsThe island showed him the monuments built before the sea swallowed the plains.Circles of stone aligned with stars.
Standing stones marking seasons.
Burial chambers echoing drumbeats.
Spirals carved into rock, showing water and wind.Then the climate changed again.
Rains shifted.
Herds vanished.
The monuments were abandoned.But the knowledge remained — carried into the islands like embers.Lionel felt the weight of those stones in his bones.

VI. The First ListenerMist thickened around him.He saw the first Listener — a child who heard the island’s voice in tremor and tide, in neon fish and shifting mist.
She stood alone at the mud pool, listening to the volcano’s breath.Her role was simple:Hear the island before it erupts.
Save the people.
Die when the next Listener rises.Lionel felt her presence beside him, as if she still walked the clearing.

VII. The Cycle BeginsThe island showed him the first choosing — five children standing in a line, trembling, hopeful, unaware.Only one survived.
The others died in mist, in forest, in tide, in tremor.This was not cruelty.
It was ancestral memory — the echo of ancient childhood mortality.Lionel felt the familiar ache in his chest.
He had trained three cycles.
He had watched twelve children die.
He had known each death before it happened.And now, five more waited for him.

VIII. The Present

The mist thinned.
The island released him from its memory.Lionel opened his eyes.Five children stood at the edge of the clearing:Tala, sensing the mist before it movedNeme, bold and restlessSuri, memorising every detailKaro, tracking the forest’s breathLina, humming softly to steady her fearLionel watched them without speaking.He already knew Lina would survive.
He already knew the others would die.
He already knew he would die when Lina ascended.The mud pool hissed again — a warning, a reminder, a heartbeat.The cycle had begun.

Mist clung low to the roots of the forest, rolling in slow breaths across the earth.
Lionel stood at the edge of the clearing, listening to the island breathe.
The mud pool behind him hissed in uneven rhythms, each bubble rising like a heartbeat.
He had felt tremors all morning — faint, but insistent.
The island was remembering.He closed his eyes, and as he always did at the start of a new cycle, he let the island pull him backward through time.I. Before IslandsLong before Lionel’s birth, before the sea rose and broke the world into pieces, the people lived in swamp‑black nights.
They huddled around fire because fire was the only thing that held back the dark.

ONE — THE MEMORY OF FIRE

item.title: Losing Pluto
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded: When I was a science teacher , the national Curriculum for Science insisted that there were 9 planets in our solar system and that they had an ordr from the Sun, and that children needed to know and retain that fact. We came up with crazy rhymes to lean , like : My Very Easy Method Just Set Up Nine Planets Many Vile Earthlings Munch Jam Sandwiches Under Newspaper Piles, even encouraging children to make up their own ideas. These nmnemonics, where the first letters of each word represented the first letter of each planet,  namely Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars; Jupiter Saturn Neptune and Pluto. Around the 2000's , rumours started out that Pluto was for the chop. It wasn't the first time a "planet" had been culled from the list, as Ceres was considered a planet and then in 1850, it was given the chop. Today, It is considered a "dwarf planet" Well all this got me wondering. What is a planet? How do we know the difference between Ceres or Pluto or Earth, or even our Moon? a quick glnce at Wikipedia and hey presto the knowledge is aquired. it seems that planets have a big enough mass for gravity to pull them into a spherical (or near spherical) shape. Ok, that's easy to understand. It also has to have a big enough gravity to have cleared the zone of other bodies, (so there shouldn't be an asteroid field in the orbit, for example) .So Pluto gets culled on this point, as does Ceres. And for pluto, another dwarf planet, Eris ,was found in 2005 which was bigger than Pluto. At first they said 10 planets, then they got together and decided that they would intorduce the term dwarf planet. Anyway, since then, the UK govenrment changed the Key Stage 3 guidance to make it much less prescriptive and today it looks like this Students must know:   Space physics  gravity force, weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g), on Earth g=10 N/kg, different on other planets and stars; gravity forces between Earth and Moon, and between Earth and Sun (qualitative only)  our Sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy, other galaxies  the seasons and the Earth’s tilt, day length at different times of year, in different hemispheres  the light year as a unit of astronomical distance.   So what happened to Pluto, I hear you ask.Well he lives with Micky and his friends! No really, its a dwarf planet out in the far reaches of cold space. And students don't need to know the names of the planets or their order anymore.

item.title: 2nd June. Insertion of the catheter.
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
I got to the hospital for ten to seven, a bit before maybe. My wife squeezed my hand, the lines in her face from worry bleached out by sadness. We walked to the big , domed building, the hospital is old and the shell is from 1840. We get to the correct department, follow the orange flashes on the floor. Like Dorothy, following the yellow brick road to Oz.
The nurse tells us the room number. Room 101. I think of Winston Smith immediately, and the rats tied to his face. I'll tell them anything they want to know!
We sit, hold hands, waiting.Time ticks on, we joke, try to make light of the situation. The nurse tells us we are first up, and at 8.00 I kiss my wife goodbye and she bravely goes to work. I've already undressed and yes, my arse is already hanging out of the gown. There goes my dignity. Off they take me, through a maze of corridors. Finally I'm in a huge waiting space. The kind nurses take my temperature and blood pressure, and put a drip line in.Then at 8:30 they wheel me into a huge operating block. There is a big lamp hanging from the ceiling, silver and white. It's really cold! They put a fan which blows hot air under the bed covers next to me. We wait for the anesthetist. She comes, and at 8:38 I get some gas. A cold liquid is injected into my arm. I feel dizzy. Then suddenly I feel very confused, and try to resist. I remember my legs flexing, and trying to resist!
I wake up, its 1130.It takes until 12 until I'm coherent. I tell the nurse she has beautiful earrings. It's because they gave me 3 grams of morphine for the pain. I get wheeled back to room 101 and phone my wife. She's been rather worried, but she's happy to hear my voice, and I to hear hers.
Time ticks by; I count the squares on the floor, on the ceiling, drift in and out of consciousness, feel the pain stab and go.
My wife comes to pick me up. The doctor visits and tells me to take it easy. We get all the paperwork we'll need, and then my wife helps me into a wheelchair and lugs me to the car. In the car I vomit. Its Niagara Falls vomit, caused by the morphine.
Then we go home. I phone my mum and dad, give our little boy a cuddle and go to bed. He's made a picture for me, daddy attached to the machine.
Today I've done nothing. Just shared the room with my "friend" the fly, who zooms into my hair.Buzzes and annoys me. I need a wash, and to brush my teeth!. But I'm slowly getting better, and I'm lucky to have had the operation, and to have such super friends and family, and such a wonderful, beautiful wife.
The wound will heal, and the 13th the will check the plaster. Lets hope its lucky 13!
Fatigue comes and goes, as does the pain. My shoulders are stiff and sore, and my intestines are having a musical party.
Ah well, tomorrow is another day.

item.title: Learning dialysis
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Today I spent the morning learning to use the peritoneal dialysis technique, which involves masks, soap, alcohol soap, clean tables,and weighing the volume of liquid that goes in and out, waiting, checking blood pressure and weight, emptying the liquid and checking how much, filling up again, and then waiting more before finally emptying again. The nurses are very kind and patient, as are the other patients who swap stories and add encouragement. I don't feel so alone anymore.
Its not painful and I think I getting the hang of it all. Tomorrow I'll learn the cycler and the automatic method.
The stitches are out now and my scar is healing, and I can change the dressing myself.
I'm a bit tired, so I'll leave it there.

item.title: Disability
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Disability
It’s always Sunday for butterflies
They watch the beauty of creation every day
It’s always Sundays for Dolmens
They watch the grass grow and the birds fly
It’s always Sunday waiting for the post
Never comes and you wait
Waiting for the card that gives you
Acknowledgement of 80%
80% disabled. As if that means anything
Connect to the machine and hope you don’t leak
It doesn’t work and they add a new catheter.
Then a fistula
Then when they can finally clean your blood
You thank them for their help
And thank the system for its work
And thank chance you are being treated
And think about the people who aren’t
Because they live elsewhere.
They live in Sunday. With the butterflies and the Dolmens
You practice the techniques till you're perfect
Boredom perfect or numb
Inflicted on your family
They’ve spent time with worry lined faces
Holding their breath
Living in Sundays.
The day of rest.

item.title: Fitting the Jugular catheter
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
The peritoneal catheter wouldn't heal in time, it kept leaking. So with a creatinine level over 500 there weren't many options. I had to either die, or have another catheter fitted to have blood dialysis. The doctors discussed it in the room, organised it all, handed me the A4 size catheter in its sterile box, and off we go. My wife organises the cases, and checks the train times; I won't be able to drive after, so taking the car is a no-no. Tom and I catch the train, its the school holidays. He's excited, looking out the window. He loves trains. He knows I have to go to hospital, but he's happy, untouched, I hope, by this. We go past windmills, smock mills, castles , the Loire, and into Angers.
The train pulls in, and my wife arrives to pick us up from her work. She drops me off in the clinic, we sit, hold hands, and hope. I go off to see the anesthetist, she hold my hand, then kisses me goodbye. She goes back home with Tom. I get ready in my room. A nurse comes, Betadine scrub and shave. All the carers are super. Sleep.
Thursday morning comes, 09:45, we go to theatre. They give me an awful tasting drug , bitter and salty. It's a calming thing. Then, they wheel me into the waiting part, insert a drip. Then into the theatre, big, cold, with a big lamp. I don't know why, but I cant remember anything until 11.00, when I slowly wake up.
There's a nurse, she's young, hair tied up, under her paper hat. Her glasses are strange, one side is a different colour to the other, made from clip-on sides, so popular in France. I'm indiscreet and try to make conversation, asking her how long she's been a nurse, and if she has a family. She gives me a black look! Oh dear! My usual tact! Later, she comes back, and I apologise for my indiscretions and explain I was just trying to make conversation and that its none of my business. She hears me out, she asks about my family, and I tell her about Tom, and Caroline. It seems better. When I asked her about her family, there was a sadness and pain in her eyes. Sometimes we forget the human act, reaching too far.
Later, she helps the ambulance guys wheel me out. They get stuck in the sliding glass doors, and she laughs.
I go off to dialysis. In the ambulance, I'm looking out the back door, so the road seems unknown and strange, however I know the road off by heart, but I've never seen it backwards.
I get to the dialysis centre. They wheel me in and eventually, they connect me to the machine. The nurse is really experienced, takes everything in hand. It's pretty weird seeing your own blood disappear into a machine, so I try not to look. The doctor comes.The room is full of patients on dialysis, all much older than me.
I'm cold, and ask for a blanket. I'm doing OK. Then, a big wave of nausea hits me. I try to find the alarm button, and then just shout . They come, and I'm sick into a paper kidney dish. I explain I couldn't find the alarm button. The nurse points, its under my hand; I cry a bit, failing even the simplest of tasks. Is it the drugs wearing off? I vomit, and they stop the treatment. Back home. Sore, and tired, dazed. My wife picks me up and we go off. She's been worried all day. We go back. My sister and brother in law come with their children, they've kindly looked after Tom for the night.
I go to lie down.its been a long day.
Try again on Saturday.

item.title: Summer thoughts
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
I was walking across the grass today, with a sinking stomach and a sense of nausea. The grass was scattered here and there by clover flowers and leaves, pink, white and brown. Daisy heads fluttered above the short cut turf, which sprang back through each step, almost as if I was walking backwards, almost as if it was helping me to walk. The spongy mousse of the turf, full of the promise of spring; it’s a windy day, with the green leaves dancing rippling in the wind, some kind of crazy football stadium dance, the wind send the ivy leaves on the wall rippling and waving, their long branches hanging to life, seeking the sun or high fiving the clouds .I sit and struggle to think what will be, what was, what could be and what could have been. My eyes were stinging from lack of sleep, or maybe too much sleep. Smoking room, waiting room, train station smoke filled blue hazed room from the 1950’s eyes. I was so confused, lost in the woods of life, wondering at all these questions, wondering if anyone knew the answers. Of course, great people take life by the horns, and mold and mend, forge and fight. But all too often they see the responsibility of their actions in their twilight years, or not at all, and the consequences of their actions are not really noticed until long after their demise. We are all temporary, and as such, our influences should be so too. Like the big cycle of the stars, moving through the night sky, we wander through life, grasping at comfort as ants to leaves on the stream of life. Lie on the log, let the river run its course. It knows the way to the sea, and if you end up breached in life’s backwaters, enjoy the scenery. Too much of my life has been spent worrying about what will happen now. The nextness of life. Who will govern us now, or who will be our manager, or where the next 5 Euros will come from. Searching for that truth, when all the time I was surrounded by it. One thing’s for sure, now I can take a step back and really look at life’s pathways, and decide which one to take. If I take the path less travelled by, I don’t think it will be such a bad thing. Indeed is there such a path? Frost was sure, Gerard Manley Hopkins said that the plough was sharpened by the ploughing. They never saw the heave and toil of the ploughman, or maybe they did and marveled at it instead of feeling the fear in his chest. The clip clop in the corridor reminds me that the next student will be here soon. She’s already late, already the clip clop echoes in the hallway. She smiles, says hello, smells of patchouli oil and hand cream. Today she has painted nails, her blue eyes flit, she takes her diary out, and the lesson begins. Slowly she plods through the text, stumbling here and there, reading the words like so many others before her, correcting herself. She reads, without expression, concentrating on the syllables. Her glasses are lattice, designer and scarlet. She struggles with numbers, like a dancer on ice, slipping and sliding, newborn baby calf, shaking like a leaf. BREAK After, or before, I can’t remember when, when I was calm, and things lost their edge and keenness, and the ache in my chest stopped, and the blood pounding in my ears went away. I thought clearly. If the boss’ daughter runs the company, then we’ll all be out of a job within two years. We can’t rely on others for our work, but only on ourselves, it is through our own efforts that things get done. If I don’t do things then they won’t get done. I knew already though. She’d run companies before, and put them in the dustbin. She’d get given the company when her dad retires but these things are never what we want. It’s always a hassle after, and the expectations and the reality are not the same. When we get given these things, we are pleased for a short time, as one is ‘happy’ to ‘succeed’ and then we see that there is a price to pay. She’ll see that the business should have been sold to someone, or an investor should have been found. When you lose something given for free it hurts more.
The pain in my chest is quite sharp now, thumping away, burning my side. Ten years of work for that! If I calculate the money they earned off my back it’s depressing. One could say I’m lucky to have a job, or that the sadness isn’t at the gap of where I am now compared to where I would like to be, but the belief that there is a gap at all. All my life I’ve reached forward to what should be hoped, dreamed. Too much maybe, of my life, is spent daydreaming, imagining things that are flights of fancy. I walked back from the appointment, the first time I’ve walked anywhere for a while. Exploring Angers, I was lucky enough to stumble on almost the quickest way back to the office. The houses were old, all built before the second world war, homes for workers in factories long closed, or students in schools long ago. The temporary nature of a town, built around industries long since vanished. The rail links and tramway lines remain, ghost stations to factories in China. Planned a town around those industries, but forgot that companies are temporary. BREAK A city is a place whose hinterland is big enough to allow people to become specialists, to develop skills and to live from that specialty. This is being undermined by the globality of the market. BREAK They gave money to the banks to stop the crash, at 0.5% interest, and the banks invested it at 4% instead of pumping into struggling companies. Indeed, they bought shares in the competitors, or hedged positions that favoured the failure of companies, even cheating on rate transactions and generally fiddling the books. Banks, the vanguard of financial morality had become soaked in filthy lucre, forgetting their social role. Crowdfunding came into play, and will become increasingly popular as banks no longer play any role.
BREAK Its very weird to see your blood go into a machine. Bright red and bubbling. Stuck. And then the nausea kicks in. We stop, and try again on Saturday.

item.title: The Owl
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded: I heard the owl in the darkness Its eerie cry, screech and hoot Cutting through the silence Writing even though it hurts Cutting through the flesh Sting into the soul Pecking away like a fag burn Smoldering, those dark circles Distant, burnt, ember edged Faded and crackled, washed up Swept away by the owl Out to the sky and its invisible currents The pain comes with the nausea Lifting the arms to write Hooting in the night The invisible owl.

item.title: Remembering the beginnings.The Medway Poets.
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
When I was 16 or 17, perhaps a little older, around 1986/1987, while we were students at what was Rochester Tutors, my brother and I would go to the Old Town Hall, in Chatham and read our poems every week. Our dad would drive us, dropping us off at the town hall, behind an old cemetery. We were probably still listening to Punk music, listening to bands like Dead Kennedy's and The Sex Pistols, we were young and naive.
Here would be a collection of poets, and artists, including Charles Thompson (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Thomson_(artist)#The_Medway_Poets) and Sexton Ming (whose name was remarkable!) as well as Billy Childish and others would gather and read there poems. We would turn up, breathe in, stand up and dare to read our poems. People clapped or laughed, or ignored or even respected our attempts. I remember poems about Benson's and Hedges and thin end of wedges, and the Thames being full of effluent.
People would come and ask Charles Thompson about publication advice, or copyright issues, he gave his time.
We went many times, perhaps over a period of years, but were never in the limelight like Tracy Emin. Eventually, around 1988/1989 we went off to University and stopped going.
Later my brother went to university, where he did English and then Children's literature at master's level, and he now teaches this at a private school,and I drifted to science, coming back to English as an adult. I currently teach English writing at UCO and St Edward's University, Angers, as well as training business people in local businesses.

Anyway, looking back at this time stirs many memories, and I still think we were really brave to stand up and read our poems, certainly my heart beat rose, when none of or friends (who just thought it bonkers!) thought poems were cool. And today some of those Medway Poets have become internationally famous. But I must stop basking in their reflected glory.
I can't claim to have been a key member of their group, or even in their group, we were planets in the outer reaches of their solar system, drifting on our own course. And The Medway Poets (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Medway_Poets) had been going as a group for over ten years when we turned up!

I recently found a dusty file full of my poems, written between 1980 and 1990, all terrible, written in earnest, written in hope. There was even a book with a hand drawn title page, 70 poems in all. I even typed them out, on paper, rather pompously.

Here is a poem from way back then. Charles Thomson (his work can be seen here http://www.stuckismphotography.com/pages/charles.html) and my brother helped write this one, and Kirsten (my then friend and co-student at Rochester Tutor's) re-read and corrected the (many!) spelling mistakes, so I can't claim it's all my own work. Bear in mind the summer job that year for my brother was raspberry picking, which he hated, as you can see from the poem. We were young, so go easy!

Written around the mid/late 1980's, perhaps around summer 1986

THE GRIM RASPBERRY REAPER

The grim raspberry reaper is back in town
He beats up the other raspberry pickers
Working for 50p an hour
HE PUTS BRICKS IN THE BOXES
More weight, more cash
The grim raspberry reaper gorges
A tray of pest ridden raspberries
"Like eating pots of grease , like drinking pints of phlegm"
Look at the grim raspberry reaper
Look at the rooting , tooting raspberry pickers
Look at the grim raspberry reaper booting rooting tooting raspberry pickers

Don't worry about capital punishment
Just send 'em raspberry picking
The pickers are getting angry now
There is going to be a riot
The grim raspberry reaper gives them electric shock treatment
The grim raspberry reaper annihilates the raspberry pickers
He recruits more and more raspberry pickers
Never go raspberry picking
Never eat raspberries

(This statement has been issued on behalf of the national board for the promotion of Kiwi fruit)

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: In October 2020, there is an exhibition of The Medway Poets with a discussion and poetry reading at the Chatham Archive Centre.
Thanks Charles!
