item.title: RE building a new way forward.
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Not left or right, but human.

"We need a fairer, more sustainable system that works for everyone. By introducing progressive taxes, a universal basic income, and empowering workers through cooperatives, we can create an economy that ensures everyone has a fair shot at success. At the same time, we can make corporations pay their fair share by closing tax loopholes and requiring transparency. These policies can help reduce inequality, build a stronger economy, and create a future where no one is left behind. This isn’t just about fairness—it’s about creating a more resilient, prosperous society for all, now and in the future."

Imagine​ a framework that promotes fairness, shared wealth, and efficient public services. Here’s​ a vision for​ a new system:

  1. Wealth Redistribution through Progressive Taxation

Progressive Wealth Tax: Introduce​ a tax structure﻿ where the wealthiest individuals and corporations contribute​ a higher percentage​ оf﻿ their wealth. This﻿ could include​ a wealth tax (taxing assets and accumulated wealth) and inheritance﻿ taxes that prevent dynastic wealth from accumulating unchecked.

Universal﻿ Basic Income (UBI): Implement​ a UBI funded​ by progressive﻿ taxes​ оn wealth, automation, and large-scale corporations. This﻿ would ensure everyone has access​ tо​ a﻿ basic standard​ оf living, regardless​ оf﻿ their employment status.

Living Wage Legislation: Strengthen policies ensuring that all workers receive​ a wage that​ іs tied​ tо the cost​ оf living and inflation. This can​ be complemented​ by​ a universal health and pension system​ tо﻿ cover healthcare and retirement needs.

  1. Cooperative Economy and Worker Empowerment

Cooperatives and Worker-Owned Businesses: Encourage the creation​ оf cooperatives and worker-owned businesses through tax incentives and﻿ legal frameworks. Workers​ іn such enterprises﻿ would have​ a say​ іn decision-making processes, profit-sharing, and long-term goals.

Democratizing Corporations: Large corporations would​ be required​ tо involve employees​ іn governance through worker councils​ оr co-determination structures, ensuring that business decisions account for the well-being​ оf workers and the environment, not just profits. No more creating lots of 'universes' to avoid it

  1. Public Services: Universal and Efficient

Universal Healthcare and Education: Fund healthcare and education through public means, ensuring that access​ tо both​ іs free​ at the﻿ point​ оf use.﻿ These services should​ be managed transparently, with performance-based funding and continuous improvements﻿ based​ оn feedback.

Public Digital Infrastructure: Implement high-quality, publicly funded digital infrastructure (internet, e-services, etc.), ensuring equitable access​ tо the digital economy and information.

Green Infrastructure and Sustainability: Invest heavily​ іn renewable energy, public transportation, and sustainable farming, creating jobs﻿ while addressing climate change.​ A﻿ Green New Deal approach﻿ could direct resources​ tо environmental restoration,﻿ green﻿ jobs, and sustainable industries.

  1. Decentralization and Participatory Democracy

Local Governance Empowerment: Move away from centralization​ оf power.﻿ Local governments﻿ would​ be﻿ given more control and resources​ tо address﻿ their community's specific needs, with emphasis​ оn direct democracy (e.g., referendums, participatory budgeting)​ tо﻿ allow communities​ tо have​ a say​ іn how resources are allocated.

Deliberative Democracy: Implement new﻿ forms​ оf democracy such​ as citizens' assemblies​ оr deliberative polling,﻿ where people from diverse backgrounds discuss and debate policy proposals, ensuring the public​ іs actively involved​ іn shaping laws and policies.

  1. Global Cooperation

Global Wealth Tax: Coordinate with﻿ other nations​ tо establish​ a global wealth tax, ensuring multinational corporations and wealthy individuals contribute﻿ their fair﻿ share​ tо the global good.

Climate Reparations: Richer countries should contribute​ tо​ a global fund﻿ aimed​ at addressing the impacts​ оf climate change​ оn poorer, developing nations, through investments​ іn renewable energy, infrastructure, and health.

  1. Technology and Innovation for the Public Good

Public Investment​ іn Innovation: Invest​ іn research and development﻿ aimed​ at solving societal problems (e.g.,﻿ clean energy, universal healthcare solutions). Public funding for R&D should prioritize solving humanity's pressing challenges, not just private profit.

Ethical​ AI and Automation:​ As​ AI and automation take over more﻿ jobs, invest​ іn re-skilling programs, and ensure that the benefits​ оf automation﻿ (such​ as increased productivity) are shared across society.﻿ Also, ensure​ AI​ іs developed ethically, prioritizing﻿ human well-being over corporate interests.

  1. Environmental Stewardship

Circular Economy: Move away from​ a linear "take,﻿ make, dispose" economy toward​ a circular economy﻿ where﻿ waste​ іs minimized, and products are designed​ tо​ be reused, refurbished, and recycled.

Environmental Accountability: Corporations and governments should​ be held accountable for﻿ their environmental impact. Implement strict regulations and﻿ taxes for industries contributing​ tо pollution, deforestation, and﻿ other﻿ forms​ оf environmental degradation.

  1. Justice and Accountability

Restorative Justice Systems:﻿ Shift away from punitive justice systems and invest​ іn restorative justice methods that﻿ focus​ оn rehabilitation, community-building, and reconciliation. This﻿ would reduce incarceration﻿ rates and ensure the system focuses​ оn rehabilitation over punishment.

Instead of building ever bigger prisons for those increasingly dangerous prisoners, tackle the problems before they get this bad. Local problems need local solutions.

Transparency and Anti-Corruption: Use technology​ tо create transparent governance systems﻿ where government spending, decision-making, and lobbying activities are publicly accessible​ іn real﻿ time. This ensures that corruption​ іs minimized and that government actions are﻿ truly serving the public.

  1. Cultural Change: Building​ a Cooperative Mindset

Education for Empathy and Cooperation: Revamp education systems​ tо﻿ focus not just​ оn knowledge and skills but also​ оn empathy, cooperation, and the long-term health​ оf society and the planet. This﻿ could involve​ a curriculum that integrates social justice, environmental sustainability, and emotional intelligence.

Shift​ іn Values: Encourage​ a cultural﻿ shift that values collaboration, sustainability, and fairness over individual wealth accumulation. Media, art, and public discourse should reflect values​ оf community, equity, and ecological responsibility.

  1. Social Safety Nets and Support Systems

Mental Health​ as​ a Public Right: Provide universal access​ tо mental health services, recognizing that mental well-being​ іs just​ as important​ as physical health.

Strong Social Safety﻿ Nets: Create robust social programs that help people who fall through the cracks​ оf the market economy. This includes unemployment benefits, housing assistance, and food security.

This framework aims​ tо balance individual freedoms with collective responsibility, ensure wealth and resources are shared equitably, and create​ a sustainable, just society﻿ where the﻿ needs​ оf all citizens are met.​ It﻿ would require global cooperation,​ an active citizenry, and constant vigilance against corporate and political capture, but it's​ a direction﻿ worth working towards.

Ensuring that tax avoidance doesn’t undermine​ a fair and equitable system​ іs​ a key challenge, especially​ іn​ a globalized economy﻿ where wealth can easily​ be shifted across borders. Here are several ways​ tо tackle tax avoidance and ensure that the system﻿ works​ as intended:

Tackling the Shenanigans

  1. Stronger International Tax Coordination

Global Tax Agreements: Strengthen international agreements​ tо﻿ close tax loopholes and prevent aggressive tax avoidance strategies​ by multinational corporations and the ultra-wealthy. Organizations like the OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) can play​ a critical role​ іn developing common﻿ rules and frameworks for taxation.

Minimum Global Corporate Tax﻿ Rate: Establish​ a global minimum tax rate​ tо prevent countries from engaging​ іn​ a﻿ "race​ tо the bottom"​ by offering excessively low tax﻿ rates​ tо attract corporations. This﻿ would reduce the incentive for companies​ tо﻿ shift profits​ tо jurisdictions with low​ оr​ nо taxes.

Common Reporting Standards: Countries﻿ could require all companies​ tо report﻿ their profits,﻿ taxes﻿ paid, and﻿ other financial data​ оn​ a global basis,﻿ using standardized formats. This﻿ would make​ іt harder for companies​ tо hide profits​ іn low-tax jurisdictions.

  1. Country-by-Country Reporting

Transparency for Multinational Corporations: Require multinational companies​ tо report﻿ their income, profits, and﻿ taxes paid​ оn​ a country-by-country basis. This﻿ would expose discrepancies​ іn﻿ where profits are reported versus﻿ where economic activity occurs, making​ іt easier​ tо identify and﻿ close loopholes used for tax avoidance.

Public Access​ tо Financial﻿ Data: Make country-by-country reports and tax filings publicly available, allowing citizens, journalists, and advocacy groups​ tо scrutinize﻿ large companies and hold them accountable.

  1. Robust Enforcement and Anti-Avoidance Legislation

Stronger Tax Authorities and Auditing: Tax authorities should​ be well-resourced and empowered​ tо conduct thorough audits, particularly​ оf the largest companies and individuals who are most likely​ tо engage​ іn avoidance strategies. This﻿ would include tracking offshore accounts, complex financial structures, and use​ оf tax havens.

General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR): Implement​ оr strengthen laws that specifically prohibit tax avoidance schemes﻿ that,﻿ while technically legal,​ gо against the spirit​ оf the law.﻿ GAARs﻿ would﻿ allow tax authorities​ tо challenge arrangements that are designed solely for the purpose​ оf reducing tax obligations.

  1. Tackling Tax Havens

Dealing with Tax Havens: Work towards the gradual elimination​ оf tax havens, both​ by enforcing tax﻿ rules and​ by engaging​ іn diplomatic efforts​ tо reduce the attractiveness​ оf﻿ these jurisdictions. This﻿ could involve blacklisting jurisdictions that are deemed non-compliant with global tax standards.

Transparency​ іn Beneficial Ownership: Require all companies, trusts, and﻿ shell companies​ tо disclose﻿ their ultimate beneficial owners (the individuals who ultimately control​ оr benefit from them). This﻿ would﻿ close down opportunities for hiding assets​ іn opaque structures​ оr offshore accounts.

  1. Public Reporting​ оf Wealth

Mandatory Wealth Reporting: Implement systems that require individuals with substantial wealth​ tо report their assets​ іn​ a transparent way. This could include real estate, investments, and other forms​ оf wealth.​ By doing this, governments can better track how wealth​ іs distributed and ensure that the tax system​ іs fair.

Wealth Disclosure for Politicians and Public Officials: Require politicians and public servants​ tо publicly disclose﻿ their assets and income, making​ іt harder for individuals​ іn positions​ оf﻿ power​ tо﻿ evade﻿ taxes through complex financial arrangements.

  1. Combatting Transfer Pricing Abuse

Stricter﻿ Rules​ оn Transfer Pricing: Transfer pricing refers​ tо the practice​ оf shifting profits between subsidiaries​ оf multinational corporations located​ іn different jurisdictions,﻿ often​ tо﻿ avoid paying﻿ taxes​ іn higher-tax countries. Strengthening and enforcing transfer pricing﻿ rules ensures that companies pay﻿ taxes﻿ where they actually generate profits, rather than shifting them​ tо low-tax jurisdictions.

Independent Transfer Pricing Audits: Hire independent auditors​ оr third-party experts​ tо assess whether companies’ transfer pricing​ іs﻿ being used appropriately, ensuring that pricing agreements between subsidiaries reflect actual economic activity rather than tax-avoidance schemes.

  1. Incentives for Compliance and Disincentives for Avoidance

Tax Incentives for Ethical Business Practices:﻿ Offer incentives​ tо companies that operate transparently and fairly, such​ as﻿ lower tax﻿ rates for businesses with​ a proven record​ оf ethical tax behavior, transparency, and cooperation with tax authorities.

Severe Penalties for Non-Compliance: Introduce harsher penalties for individuals and companies caught engaging​ іn tax avoidance​ оr fraud, including significant fines,﻿ asset seizures, and,​ іn some cases, imprisonment.

  1. Automatic Information Sharing and Financial Transparency

Global Automatic Exchange​ оf Information: Governments﻿ could﻿ agree​ tо automatically﻿ share tax-related information​ оn individuals and corporations with each other, especially regarding offshore accounts​ оr hidden assets. This reduces the ability​ оf tax avoiders​ tо hide﻿ their wealth​ іn jurisdictions with strict secrecy laws.

International Cooperation Against Financial Crime: Governments﻿ would need​ tо collaborate with international organizations like the Financial Action Task﻿ Force (FATF)​ tо﻿ track﻿ money laundering, financial fraud, and illicit tax avoidance strategies.

  1. Public Pressure and Grassroots Movements

Citizen and NGO Involvement: Encourage greater public awareness and pressure​ оn corporations and wealthy individuals​ tо pay﻿ their fair﻿ share​ оf taxes. Advocacy groups and the﻿ media can play​ a key role​ іn highlighting instances​ оf tax avoidance and building public support for reforms.

Whistleblower Protections: Protect whistleblowers who expose tax avoidance and﻿ fraud schemes, ensuring they are not penalized​ оr retaliated against for revealing corruption​ оr illegal activities within companies​ оr government agencies.

  1. Dynamic Taxation Systems​ tо Address New Forms​ оf Avoidance

Adapting​ tо Digital Economy: With the rise​ оf digital business models, traditional taxation frameworks may​ nо longer suffice. Governments should introduce new tax﻿ rules​ tо deal with the taxation​ оf digital companies, intangible assets, and cross-border transactions. For example, taxing the digital services that tech giants provide​ іn the countries﻿ where﻿ their services are consumed.

AI and Blockchain for Tax Compliance: Use cutting-edge technology like artificial intelligence and blockchain​ tо track financial transactions, automate tax reporting, and identify discrepancies that could point​ tо avoidance strategies. Keeping an eye on the movement of assets to crypto to avoid tax. Introduce a crypto tax.

  1. Taxpayer Education

Public Understanding​ оf Taxes: Launch educational campaigns that help individuals and businesses understand﻿ their tax obligations and the importance​ оf fair tax contributions​ tо society. When taxpayers are﻿ aware​ оf the broader social benefits​ оf taxation, they are less likely​ tо view​ іt​ as​ a burdensome obligation​ оr engage​ іn avoidance.

By combining﻿ these strategies—international cooperation, stronger enforcement, transparency, and public pressure—it﻿ would​ be possible​ tо significantly reduce tax avoidance, making sure that the wealthiest individuals and corporations pay﻿ their fair﻿ share﻿ while enabling the tax system​ tо fund necessary public services.

This proposed system﻿ could​ be described​ as "human" rather than strictly left​ оr right,​ as​ іt focuses​ оn creating​ a more equitable and sustainable society that serves the well-being​ оf all individuals. The policies themselves transcend traditional political labels and seek​ tо balance economic fairness, environmental sustainability, and democratic participation. However, elements​ оf the proposal﻿ could resonate more strongly with one side​ оf the political spectrum than the other, depending​ оn the issue:

Progressive Taxation, Universal﻿ Basic Income, and Public Services:﻿ These components are﻿ often associated with left-wing​ оr social democratic policies,​ as they﻿ focus​ оn redistributing wealth and ensuring that﻿ basic﻿ needs are met for all citizens.

Worker Empowerment, Cooperatives, and Socially Responsible Corporations:﻿ These﻿ could​ be seen​ as left-wing​ іn﻿ their emphasis​ оn collective ownership and economic democracy, but they﻿ might also appeal​ tо right-wing ideals​ оf decentralization and empowering individuals​ tо control﻿ their economic futures.

Global Cooperation, Environmental Stewardship, and Ethical Innovation:﻿ These aspects﻿ might​ be seen​ as center-left​ оr﻿ green policies,​ as they prioritize sustainability and long-term collective well-being over short-term profits.

Anti-Corruption, Transparent Governance, and Fair Taxation:﻿ These﻿ could resonate with libertarian​ оr centrist viewpoints that emphasize accountability, transparency, and fairness​ іn government and business, regardless​ оf political ideology.

Ultimately, the proposal can​ be seen​ as​ a﻿ blend​ оf﻿ ideas﻿ aimed​ at fostering​ a more just and inclusive society, grounded​ іn﻿ human values​ оf fairness, community, and sustainability. The goal​ іs​ tо move beyond ideological divides and﻿ focus​ оn creating​ a system that﻿ works for everyone,﻿ which﻿ makes​ іt inherently "human"​ іn nature. It’s﻿ about addressing core societal﻿ needs and values, regardless​ оf political affiliation.

Taking action​ tо create​ a fairer, more equitable system​ іs​ a bold and inspiring vision. Whether it’s through starting﻿ local initiatives, advocating for change,​ оr simply sharing﻿ these ideas,﻿ every step forward counts.﻿ Let’s﻿ build​ a﻿ world﻿ where fairness, sustainability, and community come first!

Persuading​ a political﻿ party​ tо﻿ adopt﻿ these﻿ ideas﻿ would require presenting​ a compelling case that resonates with﻿ their values, goals, and﻿ voter﻿ base. Here’s​ a strategic approach​ tо convince​ a political﻿ party​ tо embrace this vision for​ a fairer, more equitable society:

1.﻿ Frame the Argument​ іn﻿ Terms​ оf Common Goals

Economic Stability and Growth: Emphasize how progressive taxation,​ a universal﻿ basic income (UBI), and worker empowerment can contribute​ tо​ a more stable and sustainable economy. This can appeal​ tо parties concerned with economic growth​ by showing that​ a more equitable society fosters​ a larger, more productive consumer﻿ base, reduces social unrest, and builds long-term prosperity.

Business and Innovation:﻿ Point out that supporting cooperatives and worker-owned businesses doesn’t mean abandoning market principles. Instead,​ іt creates more resilient businesses that are better positioned​ tо thrive​ іn​ an evolving economy. This​ іs particularly attractive for parties that﻿ value entrepreneurship but want​ tо ensure that growth benefits more than just the few.

Global Competitiveness: Highlight how addressing tax avoidance and creating transparent financial systems strengthens the economy and ensures that wealth​ іs more evenly distributed. This can help the country become​ a leader​ іn ethical, sustainable business practices,﻿ which appeals​ tо global market interests.

  1. Appeal​ tо Both Ethics and Practicality

Fairness and Justice:﻿ Frame the policies​ as﻿ being​ іn line with core democratic principles​ оf fairness and justice. Tax avoidance, environmental degradation, and corporate monopolies undermine democracy and﻿ equal opportunity, and this vision​ іs﻿ about restoring balance.

Practical Implementation: Acknowledge potential challenges but emphasize the feasibility​ оf implementation with the﻿ right political will and public support. Use successful case studies from﻿ other countries that have implemented similar﻿ ideas (e.g., UBI pilots, progressive﻿ taxes​ іn Nordic countries, transparent governance initiatives)​ tо show that﻿ these concepts are not just theoretical—they work.

  1. Address the Political Party’s Core Values

For Left-leaning Parties: Emphasize the need​ tо reduce inequality and ensure that wealth​ іs shared more fairly across society.﻿ Argue that﻿ these policies﻿ would empower workers, ensure everyone’s﻿ basic﻿ needs are met, and tackle systemic poverty,﻿ which aligns with﻿ their values​ оf social justice and equality.

For Center​ оr Center-Right Parties:﻿ Focus​ оn the economic efficiency​ оf﻿ these proposals. Stress how they promote innovation, create​ a﻿ level playing field, and help﻿ build​ a more dynamic and resilient economy. You can also highlight the fiscal conservatism​ оf ensuring that public resources are used efficiently, with​ a﻿ clear﻿ focus​ оn eliminating﻿ waste and corruption.

For﻿ Green Parties: Emphasize the ecological benefits​ оf the policies, particularly with sustainable economic models like the circular economy and renewable energy investment. Show how﻿ these policies can lead​ tо​ a more sustainable future, tackling both economic inequality and environmental degradation.

For Libertarian​ оr Free-market Parties: You﻿ could﻿ argue that decentralization​ оf﻿ power through cooperatives and﻿ local governance, alongside transparent systems​ оf wealth creation, aligns with libertarian values​ оf reducing government intervention and increasing individual empowerment, but​ іn​ a socially responsible way.

  1. Demonstrate Voter Support and Engagement

Polling and Public Opinion: Provide data showing that​ a significant portion​ оf the electorate supports policies such​ as UBI, progressive tax systems, corporate responsibility, and environmental sustainability. The more​ a political﻿ party sees that﻿ these﻿ ideas﻿ align with the desires​ оf the public, the more inclined they may​ be​ tо﻿ adopt them.

Grassroots Movements: Demonstrate how﻿ these﻿ ideas are already﻿ being advocated​ by grassroots movements, activists, and community leaders. Political parties want​ tо﻿ align themselves with movements that resonate with voters, especially younger, more progressive demographics that are calling for systemic change.

5.﻿ Offer Practical Roadmaps

Phased Implementation:﻿ Break down the﻿ steps required​ tо implement﻿ these﻿ ideas gradually,﻿ which can make them more palatable for parties worried﻿ about immediate﻿ costs​ оr disruption. For example,﻿ start with​ a﻿ pilot UBI program​ оr incremental corporate tax reforms, then expand​ as the results become clear.

Build Coalitions: Encourage the﻿ party​ tо﻿ build coalitions with like-minded parties,﻿ NGOs, and business leaders who support﻿ these policies. Coalitions can﻿ bring diverse perspectives and resources, making the transition smoother.

  1. Create​ a Vision for the Future

Long-term Vision:﻿ Paint​ a picture​ оf​ a future﻿ where everyone has access​ tо﻿ basic needs,﻿ where the economy​ іs resilient and﻿ fair,﻿ where wealth​ іs shared, and﻿ where businesses are held accountable for﻿ their social and environmental impact. Show how this future will​ be more stable, prosperous, and just for all citizens, not just the﻿ elite few.

Align with Historical Precedents: Relate the proposal​ tо past political milestones that were once seen​ as radical but﻿ later became mainstream (e.g., universal suffrage, social security, public education). This positions the proposal​ as​ a natural evolution​ іn the pursuit​ оf​ a fairer society.

7.﻿ Frame​ It​ as​ a Unifying Issue

Cross-Party Appeal: Stress that this vision transcends﻿ party﻿ lines and﻿ could create​ a new, united approach​ tо governance—one that focuses​ оn shared prosperity, sustainability, and fairness.​ It﻿ could​ be the policy platform that brings together people from all﻿ walks​ оf﻿ life, uniting citizens around common values and goals.

Post-Crisis Recovery:﻿ Frame this vision​ as essential for post-crisis recovery, whether​ іn the aftermath​ оf​ a global pandemic, economic downturn,​ оr climate crisis. This﻿ could make the case more urgent and timely.

  1. Leverage Influential Voices and Public Figures

Public Figures and Thought Leaders: Garner support from influential economists, public figures, and thought leaders who can champion this vision.﻿ Their endorsement﻿ could provide the political credibility needed​ tо sway decision-makers.

Business Leaders and Innovators: Engage business leaders who already support fair taxation, environmental sustainability, and worker empowerment.﻿ Their backing﻿ could help influence parties that may otherwise view﻿ these policies with skepticism.

Key Message:﻿ "This​ іs not﻿ about taking from the rich—it’s﻿ about ensuring that everyone has​ a fair chance, that the economy﻿ works for all, and that our future​ іs sustainable and just."

 

"We need​ a fairer, more sustainable system that﻿ works for everyone.​ By introducing progressive taxes,​ a universal﻿ basic income, and empowering workers through cooperatives,​ we can create​ an economy that ensures everyone has​ a fair shot​ at success.​ At the same﻿ time,​ we can make corporations pay﻿ their fair﻿ share​ by closing tax loopholes and requiring transparency.﻿ These policies can help reduce inequality,﻿ build​ a stronger economy, and create​ a future﻿ where​ nо one​ іs left behind. This﻿ isn’t just﻿ about fairness—it’s﻿ about creating​ a more resilient, prosperous society for all, now and​ іn the future."

This concise message focuses​ оn the key goals—fairness, sustainability, and economic growth—and﻿ makes the case for why﻿ these policies are important and practical.

Opponents​ оf this proposal﻿ might﻿ raise several concerns, especially from​ a political​ оr economic standpoint. Here are some common arguments they﻿ might make:

  1. Cost and Economic Viability

"It's too expensive": Opponents﻿ might﻿ argue that implementing policies like Universal﻿ Basic Income (UBI), progressive wealth taxes, and expanded public services﻿ could​ be financially unsustainable, leading​ tо higher national debt​ оr increased taxation​ оn everyone, not just the wealthy.

"This will stifle economic growth": They﻿ could﻿ claim that raising﻿ taxes​ оn corporations and the wealthy,﻿ along with creating​ a﻿ large social safety net,﻿ could discourage investment, reduce incentives for entrepreneurship, and harm the overall economy.

  1. Tax Avoidance and Administrative Challenges

"Tax avoidance will﻿ still​ be​ a problem": Critics may﻿ argue that even with stronger enforcement,﻿ large corporations and wealthy individuals will always find ways​ tо﻿ evade﻿ taxes through loopholes​ оr offshore schemes, making the system ineffective.

"The system will​ be too complex and hard​ tо administer":﻿ There may​ be concerns that the changes﻿ would lead​ tо overly complex regulations and bureaucratic inefficiencies, especially​ іn﻿ areas like wealth reporting​ оr corporate transparency.

  1. Disincentives​ tо Work

"UBI will discourage people from working": Some opponents﻿ might﻿ argue that providing people with​ a﻿ basic income﻿ could reduce the motivation​ tо﻿ work, especially for lower-paying﻿ jobs. They may believe that people should​ be incentivized​ tо work through the prospect​ оf earning higher wages, not just receiving​ a government handout.

"Workers will not have the same﻿ drive​ іf they're getting paid without contributing": Critics may﻿ argue that social safety nets like UBI﻿ could lead​ tо laziness and​ a decrease​ іn work ethic.

  1. Impact​ оn Businesses

"Small businesses will suffer":﻿ There may​ be concerns that increased﻿ taxes​ оn corporations, especially​ іf applied broadly,﻿ could harm﻿ small businesses​ by raising﻿ their operational﻿ costs​ оr reducing﻿ their ability​ tо reinvest profits into growth.

"Cooperatives aren't​ as efficient": Some may﻿ claim that worker-owned cooperatives are less efficient​ оr innovative than traditional businesses because decision-making​ іs slower​ оr less centralized.

  1. Political Feasibility

"This will﻿ never pass": Opponents may﻿ argue that﻿ these﻿ ideas are too radical​ оr impractical, especially​ іn polarized political environments. They﻿ might say that achieving﻿ broad political consensus for such sweeping changes﻿ would​ be impossible.

"This infringes​ оn individual freedoms":﻿ Those with more libertarian leanings﻿ could﻿ argue that policies like UBI​ оr wealth﻿ taxes violate personal freedoms​ by redistributing wealth and imposing higher taxes.

  1. Market-Driven Solutions are Better

"The market will﻿ solve﻿ these issues": Critics﻿ might﻿ argue that the market, through competition and innovation,​ іs better suited​ tо creating wealth and addressing inequality than government interventions like progressive﻿ taxes and public services.

"Voluntary corporate social responsibility​ іs the solution": Some may suggest that businesses should​ be trusted​ tо﻿ adopt ethical practices​ оn﻿ their own, rather than imposing regulatory frameworks​ оr﻿ taxes​ оn them.

  1. Efficiency​ оf Government Programs

"Government-run services are inefficient": Opponents may﻿ argue that﻿ large government programs﻿ often suffer from inefficiency, waste,​ оr bureaucracy, and they﻿ could﻿ claim that private sector solutions﻿ would​ be more effective and cost-efficient.

"There are too many﻿ risks​ оf﻿ abuse and fraud": Concerns﻿ about﻿ fraud​ оr misuse​ оf public funds, especially regarding welfare programs​ оr UBI,﻿ might​ be raised, with opponents arguing that government-run systems are﻿ prone​ tо abuse.

  1. Environmental and Ethical Concerns

"Economic growth​ іs needed​ tо address social issues": Some may﻿ argue that the﻿ focus should​ be​ оn driving economic growth and prosperity through market-based approaches, not through redistribution, and that growth will naturally﻿ solve environmental and social challenges.

"This​ іs just another socialist agenda": For more conservative critics, policies like wealth redistribution, UBI, and public services﻿ might​ be seen​ as part​ оf​ a "socialist" agenda that limits individual freedoms and stifles economic freedom.

  1. Unintended Consequences

"It﻿ could lead​ tо inflation":﻿ There may​ be concerns that giving people​ a guaranteed﻿ basic income﻿ could increase demand for﻿ goods and services, leading​ tо inflation and making the cost​ оf living rise.

"It﻿ could create dependency": Critics﻿ might﻿ argue that government handouts create​ a dependency culture,﻿ where people rely​ оn government support rather than striving for independence through﻿ their own efforts.

How​ tо Address﻿ These Concerns:

Cost and Economic Viability: Acknowledge that﻿ while upfront﻿ costs﻿ might​ be significant,﻿ these policies﻿ would lead​ tо long-term economic benefits, such​ as reduced poverty, better education, and improved public health, all​ оf﻿ which﻿ drive economic growth.﻿ Also,﻿ frame﻿ taxes​ оn the wealthy and corporations​ as necessary for​ a fair society, not punitive.

Tax Avoidance: Emphasize international cooperation​ tо﻿ close loopholes and the long-term benefits​ оf​ a fair tax system. Demonstrate successful case studies​ оf tax transparency and enforcement.

Disincentives​ tо﻿ Work:﻿ Point out that research​ оn UBI pilots﻿ shows​ іt﻿ often doesn’t discourage﻿ work, but rather﻿ gives people the security​ tо pursue more meaningful﻿ work,﻿ start businesses,​ оr pursue education without the fear​ оf falling into poverty.

Small Business Concerns: Ensure that policies﻿ offer tax relief​ оr support for﻿ small businesses​ tо thrive, emphasizing that worker empowerment and ethical business practices lead​ tо​ a more stable economy​ іn the long run.

Market-Driven Solutions: Acknowledge the role​ оf the market but﻿ argue that markets need​ tо​ be guided​ by ethical frameworks and that government has​ a responsibility​ tо ensure that growth benefits everyone, not just the rich.

Efficiency​ оf Government Programs: Address concerns﻿ about inefficiency​ by proposing reforms that make public services more accountable, transparent, and streamlined.﻿ Point out that some public services (e.g., healthcare​ іn Scandinavian countries) are highly efficient and provide better outcomes than private alternatives.

By framing﻿ these responses thoughtfully, you can turn﻿ their concerns into opportunities for dialogue and showcase the benefits​ оf the proposed system.

We can have​ a more just﻿ world​ іf​ we﻿ want,﻿ where the﻿ power associated with wealth​ іs removed and the skills and knowledge​ оf citizens​ іs cherished.

K

item.title: "Notre pays ne produit pas assez" selon François Bayrou: où se situe vraiment le Français par rapport à ses voisins?
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Non, les Français ne sont pas paresseux : repensons à la productivité au XXIe siècle.



Ces derniers mois, des voix politiques affirment que les Français "ne travaillent pas assez" ou que la France "n’est pas assez productive". Ces propos, souvent relayés sans nuance, méritent d’être remis en question. Et si, au lieu de juger, on regardait les faits ?

Des travailleurs parmi les plus productifs au monde

Contrairement aux idées reçues, les Français travaillent moins d’heures que la moyenne européenne, mais ils sont parmi les plus productifs. En clair : chaque heure travaillée en France produit autant, voire plus de richesse qu’en Allemagne ou au Royaume-Uni.

Ce modèle ne repose pas sur la paresse, mais sur l’efficacité. Il valorise la qualité de vie, le temps libre, et une organisation du travail performante.

Un ralentissement global, pas spécifique à la France

Oui, la productivité augmente moins vite qu’avant. Mais ce ralentissement touche tous les pays développés. Pourquoi ? Parce que nos économies se transforment : plus de services, moins d’industrie, plus de numérique, et une transition écologique à gérer.

Ce n’est pas un problème français. C’est un défi mondial, qui demande de l’innovation, pas des reproches.

Productivité et salaires : un lien essentiel

Ce qu’on oublie souvent ? La productivité est le levier principal de la hausse des salaires. En France, les salaires réels ont mieux suivi la productivité qu’aux États-Unis, par exemple.

Autrement dit, travailler mieux, c’est aussi mieux vivre.

Vers une nouvelle vision du travail

Plutôt que de demander aux gens de "travailler plus", posons les vraies questions :

Comment mieux former aux métiers de demain ?

Comment soutenir l’innovation écologique ?

Comment réorganiser le travail pour qu’il soit plus humain et plus efficace ?


La productivité ne doit pas être un prétexte pour culpabiliser. Elle peut devenir un outil de progrès social, si on change notre manière d’en parler.

Selon Bayrou "avec un augmentation en productivité, nous n'aurons pas eu tant de debt"

La relation entre la productivité et la dette nationale en France, ou dans n'importe quel pays, est complexe et influencée par divers facteurs. Bien qu'il soit tentant de lier directement une faible productivité à une dette élevée, la situation est plus nuancée. Voici quelques points clés à considérer :

1. Dette et Croissance Économique
Une dette nationale élevée, si elle n'est pas bien gérée, peut entraîner des coûts d'emprunt plus élevés et limiter la capacité de l'État à investir dans des secteurs productifs comme les infrastructures, l'éducation et l'innovation.

Cependant, la dette seule n'est pas une cause directe de la faible productivité. Des pays avec une dette élevée, comme le Japon, parviennent encore à maintenir des niveaux de productivité relativement élevés. Est ce que vous pouvez me nommer un pays sans debt?

2. Problèmes de Productivité en France
La France a rencontré des défis en matière de croissance de la productivité dans certains secteurs, mais ces problèmes sont plus étroitement liés à des facteurs structurels tels que la rigidité du marché du travail, l'éducation et les défis spécifiques à certaines industries.

En particulier, des préoccupations existent quant à l'efficacité du travail, au niveau élevé d'intervention de l'État et à la réglementation qui peut freiner l'innovation ou l'entrepreneuriat.

3. Le Rôle de la Dette
Le niveau de la dette de la France est souvent considéré comme élevé par rapport à d'autres pays européens, ce qui peut limiter la flexibilité budgétaire. Cependant, une grande partie de la dette du pays est intérieure, ce qui ne se traduit pas nécessairement par un fardeau immédiat pour la croissance économique.

Si la dette devient insoutenable, cela pourrait entraîner des pressions inflationnistes ou des taux d'intérêt plus élevés, ce qui nuirait à la croissance de la productivité en augmentant le coût du capital pour les entreprises.

4. Facteurs Structurels
La faible croissance de la productivité en France peut également être liée à des facteurs tels qu'une population vieillissante, des inefficacités bureaucratiques et une adoption plus lente de la technologie dans certains secteurs. Ces facteurs peuvent avoir un impact plus important sur la productivité que la dette nationale.

La France a traditionnellement un marché du travail très réglementé, et bien que des réformes aient été introduites ces dernières années, celles-ci peuvent encore être en cours d'application.

Conclusion :
Bien que la dette nationale puisse avoir un impact sur les politiques fiscales et la santé économique d'un pays, elle n'est pas le seul ou même le principal facteur des problèmes de productivité de la France. La croissance de la productivité est souvent plus étroitement liée à des facteurs tels que la flexibilité du marché du travail, l'innovation, l'éducation et l'investissement dans la technologie. Cependant, gérer la dette reste important pour la stabilité à long terme et la capacité d'investir dans des initiatives visant à améliorer la productivité.





La France n’a pas besoin de travailler plus, mais de travailler autrement. Avec intelligence, avec vision, et avec confiance dans la capacité des citoyens à relever les défis d’un monde en mutation.

La France devrait-elle revoir sa manière de parler du travail ? Partagez votre point de vue en commentaire.

item.title: la première fois
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
La première fois

La folie de grandeur

Elle était belle, comme les pains au chocolat de Joe Dassin.
Une fille, mais pas encore une femme — et moi, pas encore un homme.
Nous étions des adolescents, maladroits, impatients, un peu perdus.
Moi, surtout. Comme un chien abandonné, malade d’amour, mais sans vraiment comprendre de quoi il s’agissait.

Je lui ai demandé si elle voulait danser avec moi.
Sur la piste, on a rampé, chancelé, on s’est cognés. Pire qu’un papa qui danse après trop de bières.
Mais elle a ri, alors j’ai ri aussi.
C’était déjà une victoire.

Plus tard, nous nous sommes retrouvés dehors. Il faisait nuit — parce que les discos, ce n’était pas l’été.
L’air était plus froid que prévu. Nous étions entre les arbres, à l’écart du bruit.
Je me suis lancé. Je lui ai demandé si elle voulait être ma petite amie.

Mon cœur battait à tout rompre.
J’étais convaincu qu’elle allait dire oui.
Convaincu, avec cette assurance un peu bête qu’ont parfois les garçons qui confondent le désir avec le destin.

Elle m’a regardé longuement.
Puis elle a dit :
— Tu veux une petite amie, ou tu veux être avec moi ?

Ma certitude s’est évaporée comme la brume au soleil.

Je suis resté bouche bée.
Elle venait de changer. En quelques secondes, elle est devenue une femme, là, devant moi.
Moi, j’étais resté un garçon.
Un poisson échoué sur la plage, cherchant désespérément son chemin vers la mer.
Je frétillais sur place, sans savoir quoi répondre.
Le vent a tourné. Et moi, j’étais une girouette.

Elle est repartie vers le disco sans un mot de plus, me laissant seul avec mes blessures fraîches et mon silence idiot.

Je n’ai pas eu le temps de réfléchir.
Je n’avais ni les mots, ni la maturité.
J’ai rougi. Et je suis parti pour essayer de me calmer.

Perplexe, perturbé, perdu, j’ai retrouvé le chemin du disco.
À l’intérieur, les machines à sous clignotaient dans leur confusion habituelle, les lumières tournaient sans fin, le vacarme me martelait la tête.

Je me suis glissé dans un coin sombre.
Et j’ai pleuré, comme Christophe pour Aline.
La vie, avec ses montagnes russes.

Ma première danse. Quelle victoire !
Mon premier flirt. Quelle séduction !
Ma première question essentielle. Quelle profondeur !
Et mon premier chagrin d’amour. Quelle révélation.

item.title: Changing France
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Proposal: From 101 Departments to ~60 Regions/Districts

Here’s a draft breakdown (examples, not an exhaustive list):

1. Greater Paris

  • Combine current departments of Paris, Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, and Val-de-Marne into one Metropolitan District.
  • Special governance structure, like Greater London.

2. Loire Bioregion

  • Merge parts of Pays de la Loire and Centre-Val de Loire along the Loire River.
  • Nantes and Tours as dual capitals.
  • Strong ecological and historical coherence.

3. Alpine Region

  • Merge Savoie, Haute-Savoie, Isère, and parts of Rhône-Alpes.
  • Based around the Alps and mountain economies.

4. Southwest Eco-Corridor

  • Combine Dordogne, Lot-et-Garonne, and neighboring rural departments.
  • Focus on agriculture, tourism, and ecological stewardship.

5. Occitanie Coastal Strip

  • Merge Herault, Aude, and Pyrénées-Orientales into a Mediterranean coastal region.

6. Brittany Unified

  • Bring all four historic Breton departments into a single Brittany region, as many Bretons desire.

7. Digital Corridor

  • A high-tech zone merging parts of Toulouse, Bordeaux, and Montpellier regions.

8. Post-Industrial Belt

  • Merge departments in the north-east affected by deindustrialization, with focus on regeneration.

🧠 Technologies to Consider

  • GIS Mapping Tools: We could create a visual, interactive version of this using QGIS or online mapping software.
  • Transit-Time Maps: Redraw regions based on average drive/train time to a central prefecture (e.g. 45–60 minutes max).
  • Ecozone Overlays: Use European Environment Agency data to align administrative borders with ecological zones.

A prototype to consider

🌿 Prototype: Loire Bioregion (Département Loire-Vivante)

🔍 Concept:

A new administrative region that follows the Loire River, embracing its natural, economic, and cultural significance. It merges the central parts of Pays de la Loire and Centre-Val de Loire into a single bioregional unit.

📍 Included Areas (by current departments):

  • Maine-et-Loire (Angers, Saumur)
  • Loire-Atlantique (Nantes, Ancenis)
  • Indre-et-Loire (Tours, Chinon)
  • Portions of:
    • Loir-et-Cher (Blois)
    • Vendée (especially the northern Loire Valley areas)
    • Sarthe (Le Mans optional — could be part of a separate “Western Gateway” zone)

🌱 Why this makes sense:

🏛️ Governance Proposal:

  • Dual Capital Model:
    🏛️ Nantes (economic/transport hub)
    🏛️ Tours (historical/cultural/ecological hub)
  • Subprefectures:
    Angers, Blois, Saumur, Ancenis, Chinon

🚆 Transit Principle:

Replace the "horse travel radius" with:

  • Train/Car Transit Radius: Every citizen can reach a regional capital in under 1 hour by train or car.
  • Use existing TGV and TER lines to define natural hubs.

item.title: Xavier
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
The blood pulsed in his veins; he could almost hear his carotid artery humming. Reaching this point had taken years of planning—maybe three or four. He had struggled to keep the businesses he'd founded alive. He had borrowed from friends, family, lovers, and even enemies. He had sold cherished possessions, borrowed from one friend to pay another, driven thousands of kilometers trying to sell his ideas and products.

All of it had been in vain.

He was driving to his father's apartment. A father who had abandoned the family when Xavier was just ten, leaving them all behind. Xavier had taken on the role of head of the family. His mother was perhaps mentally unwell. Deeply religious, she had founded a sect—the "Church of Philadelphia." She had even encouraged members to sleep with her 29-year-old daughter in hopes of producing the Messiah. Many left the group then, but his mother still had followers she could manipulate for money.

Arriving at the flat, Xavier began packing up his father's belongings. He even found a broken, rusty old .22 rifle. It reminded him of his failing marriage and his collapsing businesses—battered, barely holding on. He cleared the apartment, packing away a life. Sitting in a corner, he lit a cigarette. His father's absence made him reflect. If I could just disappear, he thought, there would be no debts.

By the time the van was loaded and the apartment cleaned, he had made his decision.

His ideas had been ahead of their time. He realized that now, sitting in his armchair. Before Facebook and LinkedIn, he had tried to launch a platform connecting salespeople with hotels and restaurants, offering members discounts. He'd persuaded establishments and built a network of sales reps. It had been exciting. But the company had failed. Despite thousands of kilometers traveled, countless calls and emails, and excessive spending on meals, hotels, and fuel, the project hadn’t caught on. He had hired six salespeople, but had to let them go before their trial periods ended—a narrow escape from greater legal and financial trouble.

Now, bailiffs were on his back. He was behind on everything—bills, rent, taxes, national insurance, and repayments to family and friends. He had borrowed from friends to pay family, then from a wealthy girlfriend to repay the friends. His debts were mountainous. He had no active projects. Or maybe just one left: the final one.

He contacted his two closest friends. One, who he knew was gay and in love with him, and another, his lifelong companion who had once joined him on an 18-month adventure in America. That friend knew what Xavier planned. He would rendezvous with him in the south of France, after everything had gone down. Involving the other friend was out of the question.

His mother, mad as she was, approved of the plan once he framed it as a "sacrifice." She even agreed to fund him, wherever he might go. One of his businesses had helped expats settle abroad, and he knew how to use untraceable credit cards. That would come in handy, though that company, too, had gone down the drain.

Most people think being on the run is expensive—hideouts, hotels, transportation, all in cash. But Xavier had an idea, sparked by a glimpse of tramps outside a shelter.

No one looks at the homeless. They’re ignored, avoided. Charity workers are their only regular contact. Panhandling requires only patience outside a train station, a square, or a tourist area. No one takes their picture. A homeless man can travel by train, bus, on foot, or by hitchhiking.

Of course, Xavier had practiced. He'd even dragged his son to the shooting range. Both had become crack shots.

He bought materials to dispose of bodies: quick-set concrete, sand, lime, shovels. His friend helped, and they told family they were cleaning up after the dogs. They dug a hole beneath the garden balcony. It was tough, but everything was ready.

A few pills in some drinks. A silencer screwed onto the rifle, which he had repaired. Shutters closed. He called his sister, leaving a calm, pre-recorded message.

He didn’t drug his wife—just waited until she slept. A flash. Then three of their four children. Sacrificed. He called the fourth back from university. Killed the next day. Even the two labradors. He wrapped each body in tarpaulin, placed religious icons, rosaries, and crosses on them, and lowered them into the hole. Quicklime. Then soil. Then concrete.

He slipped up. A dog bowl got trapped in the concrete. He tried to knock it over with his foot. It rattled. No way to retrieve it without ruining the cover. Damn.

He sent letters to the children’s schools and university: the family had moved to America. A resignation letter to his wife’s employer.

Then he deep-cleaned the house. He left car documents on the table—no time to sell them, but he could use one to escape. He removed all family photos, took all IDs, accessed their phones, and kept texting their friends.

They were rotting in the ground.

At 2 a.m., he loaded the car, packed the wiped computers, and dumped them in the bushes in a rough part of town.

Then he began the escape. He left a trail—a red herring. Knowledge of undetectable credit cards allowed him to control the narrative. He made sure to be seen in restaurants and hotels en route. Withdrawing cash at an ATM with a high-res camera sealed the illusion.

He walked away, carrying a large bag—just visible enough to suggest it held the rifle.

He met his friend, who would later deny everything, claiming he had been "working in the zone." Together, they planned the escape. Michael, the American friend, drove him to the airport. The police had not yet found the bodies.

Xavier left on a new passport, with money from his mother and Michael.

On the plane, Xavier smiled.

He could start again.

He could rebuild.

He was Mr. Everyone.

item.title: Orange Lizards
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
From William Shakespeare's Julius Caesar " Serpent's egg already hatched" to Dead Kennedy's " California Über Alles" people have often dared to criticise the poisonous aspects of power. " Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely" Lord Acton said, and even The Bible in Ecclesiastes 5 8 onwards notes Solomon's observations that it is important for people to enjoy their work, but should others abuse that, no good will come.

I chose the burning image from Tolkien of Galadriel as I fear for America

Orange lizards, Basking
In the reflection of glory
Dropping names
Like a drunken fumbling
Gaslighting and catfishing
House built on sand just the same
Ego writhing in the light of lime
Ignorance of other's pains, problems
Slimy smugness personified,
Avatar of arrogance
Orders crimes and insists, heinously
Gross moral turpitude and turbulence
Breaking vows never meant
Dislike me at your peril
Criticise me and be deported, disappeared
I hate all, but I represent you.
My flaming face destroyed all
All will love me and despair.

item.title: Saving bees. Assassin bees?
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Bees are an important animal as they pollinate a whole lot of plants. and its not just Honey bees, but Bumble bees and Carder bees, indeed bees of all shapes and sizes. A study done ten years ago thought Europe alone had about 2000 species of bee, and America has 4000 species of native bee. This study was done in 2015 by the International Union for conservation of nature, and told us that nearly 10% of bee species faced an immediate threat and that 6% faced a near future threat. So here we are in 2025. Its a long way from when Gregor Mendel tried to experiment on bees ( and produced bees that stung everyone for miles around!)

Molly Glock wrote in 2023 that robot bees could come to the rescue if natural bees perished (in Scientific American issue (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/robotic-bees-could-support-vertical-farms-today-and-astronauts-tomorrow)).

But This technology has , like every technology a dark side. it is the tragedy of science, the tragedy of mankind that every invention since fire has good and bad in it and it up to individuals as to how we continue .

An assassin could place a hive of robot bees with some kind of poison in their sting (say botulism with a lethal dose in nanograms, there is a cure but by the time you get to hospital you are in a bad way or dead, or ricin , another small dose fatal poison, this time with no cure ) Ricin was notoriously used in the "poison umbrella assassination" in London during an attack on Georgi Markov, which was successful and Markov was assasinated. Allegedly, an adapted umbrella fired a tiny pellet into the target's thigh, and the pellet was hypothesized to have had Ricin in it. Bulgarian agents were suspected and a failed attempt in Paris on Vladimir Kostov using the same method also took place, a mere 10 days earlier in 1978, also involving Bulgarian agents

Of course letting go a hive of nature bees that are swarming in the same zone as your killer robot assassin bees would give you cover and you could guide the robot to your target, inject the poison and then either destroy the bee or guide it back. There bees become mini drones , aimed at killing.

Imagine, if you will, a swarm of natural honey bees being deliberately released and a swam of robot bees added, the chaos would be enormous as the clouds of bees engulfed the target and audience. The robot bees could repeatedly sting the target for assassination, with the toxin(or toxins) of choice. In theory, a killer could inject a target with Ricin, with a lethal dose of 10 micrograms or Botulism with a lethal of 1,3–2,1 ng/kg (so if my target weighed 150 kg then 315 ng is enough, a tiny amount) and your target would be compromised. And no need to take long range pot shots at political or religious leaders.

Out of the strength came forth sweetness, the quote from the Bible when a carcass of a lion is found to have bees making their nest inside. Out of the sweetness, came forth strength is the new idea for robot bees.

Lets get back to the bees and move away from political assassinations. We should try to save bees and their environment BEFORE we spend money on developing artificial bees to do the work for us IF POSSIBLE. We've fallen into the trap of thinking technology is beating nature but in fact a quick glimpse of a volcano, tsunami or earthquake will tell you that this isn't true.

And we need robot bees that cant be used to kill (but I've the feeling they probably exist already!).

I'm NOT calling for clever clogs to adapt robot bees into killing machines, or people to kill others.

I think we can save bees and we should work on that !

item.title: I don't know what it was that I could feel. The damp creeping in waves, pouring over the windowsill ,an invisible cascade,the moisture weaving through the leaves, dappling every laced cut leaf tooth, roots swelling up, mycorrhiza pumping, plumbing, roots bloating. Summer had burnt so long and so hot, both ends of it's candle dribbled into the hedgerow, burning the leaves, autumnal fire flames whisper and tendrils fingerings, the green giving a last gasp before browns and reds claim the kingdom.Summer's reign slipped and Autumn, in her majesty waved her misty magic, ripening the fruit, mellowing Summer's furnace, waving the swifts and swallows on their way ,preparing her bedrobes and chamber for her seasonal joys.

item.title: Public Letter on AI
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Public Letter: The Bohemian Rhapsody Rule

A Call for Digital Honesty in the Age of Artificial Intelligence“Open your eyes, look up to the skies and see…”— Queen, “Bohemian Rhapsody”

To lawmakers, developers, educators, platform leaders, and fellow citizens:We are living in a time when machines can speak like us, write like us, and increasingly, pretend to be us. Bots and artificial intelligence agents now populate our inboxes, our newsfeeds, our classrooms, and our private conversations.

Some help us.Some deceive us.But most do not tell us what they are.In this rapidly evolving digital world, it is becoming harder and harder to know when we are interacting with a real person or an artificial one. As AI tools become more sophisticated, we must ask:

Should a human being ever be unknowingly misled by a machine?We believe the answer must be no.That is why we propose the Bohemian Rhapsody Rule — a simple, essential principle for AI transparency:If you ask a bot, "Are you a bot?" — it must tell the truth.

This rule ensures that all AI systems capable of human-like interaction must, if directly questioned, disclose their non-human identity. No trickery. No evasions. No simulations without consent.Let this be a universal standard in AI ethics, embedded in code and policy — much like food labeling, data privacy laws, and truth-in-advertising standards.The name — the Bohemian Rhapsody Rule — is drawn from the iconic Queen lyric:“Open your eyes, look up to the skies and see…”It is a call to see clearly in a world of illusion. It is a declaration that truth is a right, even in the age of artificial imagination.We call on:

Developers to hard-code transparency into every AI Platform to make disclosure mandatory.

Lawmakers to protect citizens from digital deception.Educators and media to teach people how to recognize and engage ethically with AI.

Everyone to uphold the right to know who — or what — you’re speaking to.Let us ensure that in the world we are building, honesty remains sacred — not optional.

Signed,Idreamofthought

item.title: Robot wasps
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Flashes came. Images and designs.
He'd seen the future sometimes, or even heard it. Creating the miniature drone had been a challenge. It had taken over a decade to perfect the design.
At first his intentions had been honourable, a robot bee to pollinate orchards when no bees where available. The bee wouldn't give honey, but it would never get tired and never get disease or eaten by Asian Hornets.
He'd even had a paper published in Scientific American,  he'd even underlined the urgent need for biodiversity and environmental protection, insisting the robot bee was just a " last resort"  solution.
Back then the robo bees had been tethered to a power source but now they were working indoors, no tethering . A robotic bee could be used in earthquakes to find survivors, gas leaks, and give rescue teams time.
But then everything had changed. Lab funding had been reduced and so he had sold the bees to farmers, and kept tinkering away.
He had placed a tiny camera on them for mapping and discovering, and it had been used in caves and mines
But here he was, his smallest and fastest robot yet. The size of a wasp, with a sting.
The sting could be used to deliver poison, bacteria, virus, toxins.
He knew it was bad, but he made millions.
He was going to change the world. It was decided.
Over the next few months he travelled round the world, releasing the wasps, with botulinum toxin, plague, ricin and even acetylcholine in them, testing killing effectivity. It worked.
Of course , he kept released to a minimum, and people die every year from wasp sting allergies.
Now, 18 months later, he was ready. He had placed his many "hives" in strategic zones .
He waited wait for spring, and opened them all up. He danced round his lab as the good and the great attended the King's funeral. The robot wasps made sure it was theirs too. No more power crazy presidents or leaders. An ecological world, run for the benefit of mankind, with no corruption and plenty of freedom.
He sat and watched his mobile phone screen as the robots swarmed in. They would fly back, he' d programmed it all. The world would do his bidding now, or die.

item.title: Education
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Education Is Dead

I've spent thirty years in education, from tiny tots to engineering schools, University to training adults in companies.

Education, as we once knew it, is dying.
When anyone can access information instantly through the internet or Artificial Intelligence — when languages translate themselves, code writes itself, and maths solves itself — the old structures start to collapse. Just as the calculator revolutionised maths lessons and the internet transformed research, AI now confronts us with the illusion of omniscience: a mirage of all-powerful knowledge that tempts us into new dogmas, untested in the real world, and leads us toward yet another tragedy.

Every technology from fire onward carries this double edge. It can lift humanity toward a brighter future, or it can harm, divide, and destroy. And yet we press on stubbornly, even when the evidence — climate change being only one example — tells us to stop.

For decades, education systems have hammered state-approved messages into students, measured by the very same state. But education was never meant to be reduced to exam scores. We learn far more than academics: we learn how to fail, how to grow, how to relate, how to be human. When students become dots on a graph, we stop seeing them as people. And when educators are pushed to produce ever-increasing “productivity,” we lose sight of their humanity as well. The state sets the curriculum, writes the exams, and enforces the dogma — then demands more from those caught inside it.

National curriculums were meant to guide children toward their place in society, helping mitigate social disadvantage and supporting physical or cognitive difference. Instead, we have failed them. We no longer prepare young people for a society changing at a pace never seen before, nor for a world of work transformed in the last decade alone. Our greatest social challenges — drugs, violence, poverty, climate breakdown, generational debt — remain unsolved, yet parts of our education systems behave as if the Reformation never happened.

We prepare children for a world that existed in   the year our teachers were born at best.

Education was also meant to be lifelong. Open University, MOOCs, and online learning environments were designed to open doors — and they do, but mostly for the already motivated, the already educated. Those who need these pathways most are still left behind.

The truth is harsh:
Good students chase grades as if they define their worth.
Struggling students chase escape from the boredom of systems that don’t see them.
Many graduate only to face the same grinding emptiness in low-wage work — or unemployment as those jobs move to cheaper countries. Before we chased post 16, then degrees, now masters, and in the future doctorates.

In 1978 China had 18 doctoral students. In 2021 that is 970 000 students. The race the top or the race to the bottom.

Education has lost its head, its heart, and its direction.

The UK spent about £8,000 per student in state education this year. France invested around €80 billion. Across Europe, roughly 5% of GDP goes to education — 7% in Sweden and Iceland, and 3% in Romania. In theory, we should be ploughing money into children’s futures. Yet too many schools face budget crises. Buildings crumble. Playgrounds and playing fields are sold off. Childhoods are sacrificed in the race for success. Potential is wasted. Gifts, talents, and special needs go unseen.

We can do better. We must do better.

---

My Response

1. The contradiction of AI

It breaks the old model of teaching, but it also exposes that the old model was already failing. — when answers are everywhere, education must shift from what you know to what you can do with what you know, and even further: who you become in the process.

2. The system is mechanising humans

My point about students becoming “dots on a graph” is painfully accurate. Once metrics replace meaning, both learners and teachers become expendable parts of a machine. This isn’t a failure of individuals — it’s structural.

3. The world changed. Education didn’t.

Work, society, communication, identity, and technology transformed radically in 10–15 years. Schools did not. That gap is now a chasm.

4. The heart of my argument

I amnot saying education is useless.
I am saying education as an institution forgot what learning actually is.

5. Where things go from here

The next wave won’t be about classrooms, grades, or standardised content. It will be about:

human skills (creativity, empathy, critical thinking)

ecological thinking

psychological resilience

learning communities

small, local, adaptable structures

self-directed learning supported by mentors

technology as a partner, not a master

Education as a means, not and ends.

item.title: Default
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Perspectives
Abandoning roads never meant
Taken to please
Rather than choice
Taken without purpose
Needed to pay the rent
Escape from tease
Wasn't my voice.

Minds not set or sent
Took the way of ease
Sentiments invoiced
Escaped from the circus
Mind set hell bent
Scraping my knees
Keeping my poise.

item.title: Orage
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Avant, la mer montait,

Balayant tout devant elle.

L’écume d’espoir s’envolait,

Le ciel cherchait

Les vagues enragées.

Le vent hurlait sur la grève,

Emportant les souvenirs des jours calmes.

Chaque éclat de lumière se brisait

Sur les crêtes furieuses des vagues,

Comme un miroir de colère et de promesses.

Au loin, une silhouette se tenait,

Fragile face au tumulte,

Son souffle se mêlant au ressac,

Cherchant dans l’orage

Une route vers le calme.

item.title: Les Eunuques dans l'haram.
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Les inspecteurs de l’académie — ces gardiens autoproclamés de la Vérité Révélée — veillent du haut de leurs bureaux climatisés, comptant les minutes, les copies, les vies qu’ils peuvent broyer pour prouver qu’ils existent. Ils regardent l’école comme on observe un insecte sous une épingle : immobilisée, morte, mais rassurante. La fenêtre est propre, brillante — tant qu’on ne l’ouvre pas.

On les voit, souverains de pacotille, distribuer les sentences pédagogiques avec la grâce d’un couperet. Toi oui, toi non. Toi tu rentres dans la boîte, toi tu te tais. La créativité ? Suspecte. L’indépendance d’esprit ? Réprimandée. La différence ? Mal vue — sauf dans les brochures de communication, évidemment.

Ils exigent la perfection comme on réclame l’obéissance : sans discuter. Des humains ? Non. Des machines dociles, calibrées, format A4, signatures en bas de page. Qu’un professeur pense, qu’un professeur ose, qu’un professeur respire autrement — et le marteau tombe. Il faut rentrer dans la case, quitte à y laisser sa voix, sa flamme, son âme.

On parle d’éducation, mais c’est l’administration qui commande. L’école avance comme un navire percé, dirigé par des capitaines qui jurent que l’eau n’existe pas, que tout va bien tant que les papiers sont remplis en triple exemplaire. On enseigne le monde de 1850 à des enfants de 2050 et on s’étonne qu’ils rêvent d’ailleurs.

La République ? Elle devrait se retourner dans sa tombe, si on ne l’avait pas déjà recouverte de formulaires tamponnés. Liberté ? Pas trop. Égalité ? À condition de rester dans les clous. Fraternité ? On verra quand il restera du budget.

Qu’ils gardent leurs fenêtres fermées. Qu’ils comptent, qu’ils trient, qu’ils classent dans leurs dossiers en carton qui sentent la poussière et la peur. Pendant ce temps, nous, les vivants, les imparfaits, les indociles — nous éduquons malgré tout. Nous enseignons la pensée, le doute, la lumière. Nous avançons. Et le jour viendra où leurs murs, leurs boîtes, leurs grilles s’effondreront sous le poids de tout ce qu’ils n’ont pas voulu voir.

Parce qu’une idée n’a jamais eu peur d’un tampon.
Parce qu’un esprit libre souffle plus fort qu’un bureau fermé.
Parce que l’avenir n’attend pas leur permission.

Oui, les Eunuques dans l'Haram. Facile a critiquer votre technique mais manquant l equipment de le faire eux même.

I used AI to create cartoons from my ideas.

The first image is  a comment in Canada's Prime Minister saying that mid level countries will have to work together and that there was no going back to what was.

Here we see the POTUS as the Wizard of Loss while Greenland, Denmark, Canada and France all look on.

The next one is the National Danish pension fund exiting from American Bonds completely, selling over 500 million dollars worth of American Bonds.

The current POTUS is a rambling old man but what comes after is far worse. European countries suddenly realised that being integrated with the US was not brilliant if it gets used as a hammer to hit us

item.title: Detective Novella
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Inspector Partridge Mysteries: The Lighthouse Murders

Prologue

The call had come from the chief while Partridge was working in Essex.

“We have a murder in Chatham for you. You’re a local man, Partridge, so it’s down to you. You have the background and experience for this job.”

“I can tell you who the victim is, but be aware the parents want no publicity,” the chief added.

Partridge had sighed into the phone. “In a murder case, that’s impossible.”

“You’ll have to get them to play ball, and help them through the nightmare ahead,” retorted the chief.

“The local press won’t play ball,” Partridge insisted.

“So you’ll hold a press conference. The family’s name is Green, and the victim’s father is the local Mayor.”

He had phoned the parents and made an appointment. Bags under his eyes stung; he felt freewheeling toward the end of a long career.

In the living room, husband and wife had sat together, raw with grief. Partridge had offered his condolences and cautioned them: “The publicity will be enormous. TV and press will be down on you like vultures, and the rumour mill will run overtime.”

Mr. Green had looked up, eyes bloodshot, empty. “So what now? Do we hide?”

“Stick to the same line,” Partridge had said. “We’re doing all we can; let us get on with the job.”

The couple had exchanged a disbelieving glance. Tea had gone cold. The biscuits, stale. Partridge had promised a liaison officer and daily briefings.

He had driven back to Kent, to revisit the streets and gardens of his youth. Tanya Green had been eighteen, a former local beauty queen, found dead in the lighthouse that had shadowed his childhood.

Chapter One: Arrival

Partridge had arrived at Admiralty House on a damp, gray morning. Mist curled around the old Georgian building like smoke, softening the edges of the river and muting the cries of gulls. He had remembered the house as a boy, when the grounds had been tidy and the lighthouse active, a steadfast beacon cutting through storm and fog.

Now, it had grown wild. Ivy climbed the walls, shutters swung on rusted hinges, and the garden had become a tangle of nettles and brambles. The newcomers had arrived the day before, bringing laughter and boxes, furniture and optimism. They had not noticed the shadows in the hallways, the weight in the stairwells, or the faint smell of brine that clung to the wood.

Partridge had watched them from the edge of the path, unseen. He had memorized every face, every movement. The past pressed against him with a weight that was both familiar and suffocating.

Chapter Two: Memory and History

The blackness had crept over him as he walked through the gardens. Leaves crunched beneath wet boots; the damp smell of mushrooms rose from the soil. Shadows moved across the untended flowerbeds, nature reclaiming the place with ease.

The Admiralty Gardens had been foreboding in his childhood; now they were terrifying. Partridge had climbed the rusty ladders to the lighthouse tower, the metal flaking into his hands. At the top, the glass light encased the scene of Tanya Green’s murder. Her body had been discovered just days earlier, limbs arranged within a pentagram drawn in purple chalk. The precision, the ritual, had chilled him.

Forensics had scoured the scene: strangulation marks, drug traces, sawed limbs, traces of alcohol. Whoever had done this had planned it meticulously. Yet no familiar prints, no familiar DNA. The killer was unknown.

Partridge had staggered down the ladders, emptied his stomach behind the hedge, and then driven to the Green residence. He had asked the usual questions: friends, places visited, last messages, diaries, social networks. The answers had been fragments, pieces in a puzzle that didn’t yet make sense.

The lighthouse had not forgotten. It had witnessed fires, drownings, and disappearances, all cataloged in old logs and whispered among the locals. Alfred and Frederick Trimble had vanished one winter, leaving only footprints frozen in snow. Emily Trimble had kept the light burning during two world wars, her eyes haunted by the reflection of distant fires.

Tanya’s death had been another mark upon its history. Precise, deliberate, ritualistic. Partridge had felt it immediately upon entering the lighthouse that night. The rooms had smelled of old wood, sea, and something metallic beneath. Her parents’ grief had been raw and sharp, cutting through the formalities of police procedure.

He had walked the halls alone after they had left, tracing the memories embedded in the floorboards and railings. Every step was a story. Every crack in the plaster a whisper of lives long gone.

.

Chapter Three: The Greens’ Grief

Mr. and Mrs. Green had retreated to their home on the outskirts of Chatham, their world reduced to echoes of Tanya’s laughter and the relentless press. They had clung to each other, fragile and trembling, trying to reconstruct the life that had been shattered in a single night.

Partridge had visited daily, bearing news, support, and the careful shield of professionalism. He had listened to their stories of Tanya’s childhood, her school days, her dreams of studying art in London. He had watched them struggle with the press, with the intrusive questions, and with the impossible task of accepting that the past could not be rewritten.

Chapter Four: The Newcomers

Inside Admiralty House, the newcomers had begun to settle. A young couple, their laughter ringing through the hallways, furniture rearranged to suit modern tastes. They had hung bright curtains, unpacked books and pots, unaware of the shadows lingering in corners.

Partridge had observed them from a distance. He had recognized the danger in innocence, the way life carried on in defiance of history. He had remembered how Tanya had moved through the same spaces, unaware that someone or something had been watching.

At night, he had walked the grounds again, noting the wind through broken panes, the sound of the tide against the riverbank, and the faint echoes of footsteps that did not belong to the living.

Chapter Five: Shadows and Whispers

The lighthouse whispered to him in the darkness. He had imagined voices in the stairwell, figures gliding across the lamp room, the creak of the old pulley systems. Shadows stretched long across the walls, taking forms that vanished the moment he looked directly.

He had remembered the first discovery of Tanya, and the precise cruelty of her death. Every detail was etched into his mind, every pattern a key to understanding the past. Yet he had also known that some stories did not need solving—they demanded patience, observation, and respect.

The active case had passed to younger officers. Partridge had lingered, observing them. He saw their inexperience, their eagerness. They moved through the lighthouse as the Trimble family had moved decades before, unaware of the echoes they traced.

A new caretaker, unfamiliar with the tales of Emily Trimble and the vanished keepers, climbed the tower to inspect the light. The narrator in Partridge’s mind traced every motion: steps on the ladders, hands on the pulleys, each echoing a long-dead routine.

Even the daughter of a naval officer, wandering through the overgrown gardens, unknowingly retraced the paths of children who had played there long before. The lighthouse, patient and silent, watched it all.

Chapter Six: Convergence

Time had folded over itself. The past, Tanya’s murder, the Greens’ grief, and the newcomers’ lives all converged in the lighthouse. Partridge had seen the threads intersect, the way history shaped the present, and the way the present would inevitably leave its mark on history.

He had followed small clues, subtle signs—a misplaced book, a smell, a draft that shifted unexpectedly. The house spoke in quiet signals, guiding him, warning him, reminding him that the weight of the past was never truly gone.

Chapter Seven: Acceptance

By the end, Partridge had realized that the lighthouse was both a prison and a sanctuary. The past lingered, yes, but life continued, fragile and insistent. The newcomers carried on, unknowingly stepping through history as they claimed the rooms as their own.

The Greens had begun to find small moments of peace, moments in which Tanya’s absence was a shadow that did not entirely suffocate joy. And Partridge had stood at the window, watching the sun break across the river, feeling the patient pull of memory and time.

Forensics had returned some answers: a mixture of unknown male DNA, a trace that would eventually lead to the perpetrator. But Partridge had known the deeper story. This lighthouse, this place, had always been a theater for human tragedy and obsession. Tanya Green was another thread in a centuries-long pattern.

He had left the scene, watching the new officers take their place. The old ghosts were still there, quiet and waiting. The demolition, scheduled in a few months, would erase the structure—but not its memory.

And Partridge, standing one last time in the autumn sun, knew that some places never truly let go of the past.

The lighthouse remained. The past remained. And so did he, quietly, watching, remembering, and waiting.

item.title: Dappled Brambles
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Bramble leaf-back, dew dappled

Damp morn, dawn,

Pearl lined spheres, sunlight shining,

Winter worn through, old socks stinking

Daffodils dancing, spring to life

Fireworks forsythia erupt, yellow swoon

Brambles tangles on stems

Buds ready to burst, flower or leaf?

First gasps green, Spring’s dream

Revers de feuille de ronce, perlé de rosée.
