item.title: Connection Before Content: The Three Pillars of Transformative Learning
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
For learning to be truly effective, there must first be a genuine connection with the teacher. Our school memories rarely revolve around worksheets or exams; they are about the teachers who inspired us, encouraged us, or cared enough to build a relationship with us. We remember the feeling of being seen far more than any piece of information we memorised.
As many colleagues have told me : “You have to love the students.” It sounds simple, almost obvious, but it carries a profound educational truth.


A healthy, secure rapport is not a bonus in education — it is the prerequisite. When learners feel safe, respected, and recognised, they open up. They participate. They allow curiosity to happen. Without connection, even the best content falls flat.
Some students can thrive independently, of course. But most learners need what all humans need: relationship, belonging, and attention.


Learning Begins Before School
Think back to childhood. Long before we entered a classroom, we learned to speak, walk (if able), play, interact socially, and navigate the world — all without professional educators. Parents and carers taught us these things through affection, consistency, and presence.
Connection mattered more than content. The relationship was the curriculum.
When children lack connection — when they are ignored, abandoned, or mistreated — their ability to learn is deeply compromised. No amount of curriculum can compensate for the absence of care.


The Case of Genie
Genie’s story is a heartbreaking example of what happens when a child is deprived not only of language, but of love, interaction, and human presence. Genie did not fail to learn because of a lack of intelligence; she was denied the relational environment that makes learning possible.
Her case reminds us that connection is not a luxury — it is the scaffolding upon which language, cognition, identity, and trust are built. Without it, even the strongest potential struggles to emerge.


The Three Pillars of Transformative Learning
Connection, Construction, and Conversation guide learners from feeling safe, to feeling motivated, to feeling curious.


1. Connection — Building a Link with Love
Connection is the gateway to learning. When learners feel valued, they risk engagement; when they feel unimportant or judged, they shut down. A connected learner is a receptive learner.
2. Construction — Building the Desire to Learn
Once there is connection, teachers can construct the internal motivation that drives active learning. This is where purpose and curiosity begin to grow. When learners want to learn, teaching becomes guidance, not struggle.
3. Conversation — Building the Curiosity to Question everything.

I had the chance to work with Reed Meister about a decade ago. His ideas on conversations and ethics radically changed my teaching practice. Conversations are a non violent way to explore possibilities.

Louder doesn't equal better!

How different is this to the conflict and confusion we see in current politics and education debates where everyone hangs onto broken dogma and keeps speaking to drown out the other ideas?


Conversation is where learning and education becomes transformative. Students shift from passive receivers to active co-creators of knowledge. Curiosity thrives in dialogue, not in silence or dogma.


We Need a Different Way
We cannot continue with a system that breaks both learners and teachers — and then blames them for the fractures. When students feel unseen and teachers are overwhelmed, no amount of curriculum reform will fix the deeper issue.

The fractures we cause in education go onto become the fractures in society. Instead of creating a virtuous cycle of upwards joy, we create a syphon of destruction.

Instead of passion, learners choose prison.

Instead of dynamic curiosity, learners choose drugs and crime.

Instead of love and belief, learners choose rebellion and hate.

Fail again, Fail better
This is not a failure of individuals. It is a failure of a framework that ignores the human foundations of learning: belonging, attention, and trust.

If education does not place connection at its centre, we will continue to produce burnout, boredom, and the belief that school is something to survive rather than a place to grow. The joy of learning will be lost in the drudgery of administration and compliance.


Connection is not optional. It is the foundation of all meaningful learning. It's the foundation of a healthy society and a healthy debate. It's the protection against the extemists from the right and left who want everyone to think as them.

item.title: Nordic Walking
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Last to the Top
We left Les Brûlis and climbed straight into the vines.
The rows ran long and clean, drawing the eye toward the horizon. The slope rose steadily, enough to bring the breath up. Dry earth underfoot, young leaves catching the light.
At the top, the land opened.
Sky wide and pale. The valley falling away beyond the trees. For a moment, everything held still.
We walked on toward Menhir des Pierres Meslières, the stones low and quiet among the ordered lines. Easy to miss if you didn’t know.
Then over the ridge and down.
The path narrowed into shade. Nettles brushed the edge, violets low in the grass. The ground turned stony, careful underfoot.
At the table we paused. Water. A few words. Then on.
I pushed the next climb out of habit. For a while, I was ahead.
In the final stretch they passed me—one by one, steady, stronger. I didn’t follow.
I walked.
As I climbed, they called back—small words, encouragement carried on the air. I raised a hand, kept my pace.
Back through the vines, the long lines unchanged. Slower now, I noticed more—the scent of mint, the hum of insects, the small life at the edge of the path.
A train crossed the distance, sudden and gone.
Over the crest, the light had softened. The valley remained.
I finished last.
I finished smiling.
A cool wind tonight.

item.title: American nightmares
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
If we are really honest, we’ve been watching the decline of the west for decades.

We, the west, sat on our laurels  and our world view was not that of informed people.

We learnt the world that existed the year our teachers were born.

I remember our teacher laughing in 1984 when we talked about super powers, when we suggested that China had the potential to become one. It had the population, but perhaps not the technology or the ambition. China was still a Communist country in 1984 and perhaps our teacher was right to laugh at us.

But since then China and a lot of Asia has come out of poverty. 1 billion Asians have been lifted out of poverty over the last 20 or so years.

Life expectancy has risen , technology has developed, medicine, education and the standard of living have all risen.

In China in 1978 very very few people were Doctoral candidates, now China has more doctors than most other places. They even introduced a doctorate if you produce a product, a practical PhD.

China and India seem to be outpacing the world. America is still the sprawling blob its always been, but we see the leaves turning colour, just as the British Empire post world war 1 and 2.

America has lost wars since Vietnam. You could even argue that the USA hasn’t won anything since WW2 and the emperors’ new clothes are invisible.

America went from a president who could not tell a lie, to one who could not tell the truth, and if I were to list all of Trumps alleged or even proven antics I would be here a very long time.

We saw the return of the coloseum to the white house gardens, with a fight for Trump's Birthday that left some participants bloodied and broken. Feed the crowd blood to keep them calm, it is as old as the Roman Empire.

Crew, a great source of information ( https://www.citizensforethics.org/) produced a mindboggling table here https://www.citizensforethics.org/reports-investigations/crew-reports/president-trumps-staggering-record-of-uncharged-crimes/#table which lists the problems but stops in 2023

PBS has a video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mT-WAinF2tM listing Trump's impeachable problems, including Treason.

Steven Cohen, the 9th district of Tenesee's congressman is keeping a list https://cohen.house.gov/TrumpAdminTracker

But nothing seems to happen. Trump seems teflon coated.

item.title: Death and other adventures
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Today I went to the funeral ceramony and burial of a student I taught.

He was only 19, and it was very moving. He had been shot in a road rage attack. He was waiting for his Baccalaureat results

First of all, I made my way to the Great Mosque in Nantes, as this was a Muslim ceramony.

A lot of youngsters, classmates and friends were there, with their parents, members of staff from the lycee, family and gatherers.

The ceramony itself was very quick, no songs, the Imam read his verses, prayers and suddenly it was over. Then the coffin was taken to the cemetary, where it was immediately buried. His father said some words, thanked us. His mother was devastated.

His sister, his brothers, all wept.

The funeral attendent told us that his body had been bathed and then wrapped in white linen, according to the rites of Islam, and that he would be buried and if we wanted we could say goodbye and even throw soil onto the coffin, burying him. Many people did so, i stood back and watched his friends and family do their burial. When you see the soil going onto the coffin, you know that death has done its work.

The funeral attendant thanked us all, encouraged us to come and visit the grave, to think of the decesed, plant some flow he explained that in Muslamic tradition, death is preordaned by God, so its hard, but its life. We will all go to the earth one day, he told us, but that it was especially cruel today.

May he rest in peace.

Its not the first funeral I've attended, nor the first for a young person. As I placed my hands on his father's soldiers and said meaningless words which he thanked me for, I could just think of the smile of the deceased.

I slipped away, back to the living. Many many people had come. The Mosque was full, and the graveyard too.

I staggered down the pathway , towards the cemetary gates, and I wept, thinking of the waste of it all. Today wasn't about me, however. Today wasn't about me.

item.title: The Hidden tavern (rewrite)
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
from a story https://medium.com/the-junction/the-hidden-tavern-27f508e43414 by me

THE TAVERN OF THE DEAD

The last market of October had been kind to him. He'd left the town of St. Aldric with a purse heavier than his pack — three dresses mended, a christening gown finished early, and, best of all, a wedding dress commissioned by a miller's daughter who'd wept with joy at the fitting and pressed an extra coin into his palm besides. He hummed as he walked, the coin purse knocking soft and constant against his hip, a small percussive comfort. A man could live a season on a day like that.

He'd heard talk in the market, over cider and cold meat, of a tavern further along the road — the sort that innkeepers spoke of with a strange mixture of envy and unease. Doing too well for a place so far from anywhere, someone had said. New silver on the table, new glass in the windows, and hardly a coach on that road to account for it. Another had laughed it off — envy talks, that's all, envy always finds a story — and poured more cider, and the tailor had thought no more of it. Gossip was the seasoning of every market day, and he had a wedding dress to be proud of and a purse to be careful with, and neither seemed cause for worry under an October sun.

By the time the sun failed him, he'd forgotten the warning entirely.

It was the edge of October, a dying autumn day. St. Aldric Church bells rang out their chimes on the late hour. Perhaps the next town wasn’t so far away? As the day came to a close, the last fingers of warmth left the woods. Dusk arrived, dusty and cool; mists swirled up from the ground, rising in tendrils.

The tailor emerged from the woods, stumbling and somewhat scratched by brambles and thorns. He hawked his trade from town to town, along timeless pathways. He’d started out in the late afternoon, hoping to get to the next village, but had gotten lost on the trail. The day had once been full of sunbeams and birdsong, ever welcoming, yet the scene changed as twilight tumbled. The woods were now long lost in the thick foggy sameness, a grey surround. Tree stumps littered the floor through the billowing fog.

The tailor spotted the faint lights of what he suspected was a far off village. They appeared like glowing eyes through the fog and swirled in and out of view. The tailor’s cheeks were salted with tears, having been whipped by the wind and burned by time and weather.

The path was difficult to follow, and his lantern spluttered and waved. The tailor shuffled and shivered through crisp leaves and broken branches. The lights inside a solid wooden frame blazed and he grabbed a cool iron thumb latch. Creaking like a coffin, the hinges rolled past each other. He swung open the door to the warmth and light of a tavern. He was safe.

Fear crisped from his forehead to his toes, electric, refreshing. Around the table, plates and glasses were found, as if a meal had been interrupted. A glazed ham had been half eaten, abandoned. The candles burned brightly. So many lit in a time of poverty meant a signal of some kind, or perhaps a celebration. He blew out many, keeping only a few lit so as to make it through the night. Where were the other customers?

He closed the door, which swung fast — and the terror hit him full in the stomach when he saw a single corpse swinging from the rafters, its lifeless legs wafting in an invisible wind. His breath locked. For a moment he could not move.

He forced himself to look away, scanning toward the bar for any sign of life, any explanation. As he did so, another corpse revealed itself, hanging just beyond the reach of the candlelight, its legs drifting gently as though stirred by a breath that did not exist.

The tailor turned, and there in front of him was the glinting smile of a dead man, pinned to the door. He’d been speared, gored, as if in mid-joke.

The tailor gave the sign of the cross and blew out the lantern. He hunted around in the shadows for a drink to calm his nerves. A bottle of whisky, that would do the trick. He found the slosh of a canteen full of oil. He refilled the lantern, and used his scissors to cut down the dead. There were no authorities out here in the muffled middle of nowhere. Here, the law was all too often ignored or even openly flaunted.

The inhabitants of the tavern had no documents or even any money. Some thief or highwayman had taken everything. The tailor turned to head for the stables out back. Kicking open the door, the dust climbed and stuck in his throat. A tall shadow stood in the corner — too still, too human in shape. For a heartbeat he thought it was a man waiting for him.

“Who goes there?” he cried.

A horse whinnied.

Only it remained. All the others had been taken. The surviving horse flinched in the moonless night, its shining dark coat lathered with sweat. That meant a rider had just tied it up — but whom? The tailor swung around to scan the corners. The shadows shifted with him, stretching and shrinking as if something had just stepped out of sight. But he found no one.

The tailor decided to give the dead a decent burial and get out in the morning. The murderer must have bolted when he saw him coming.

The blood swam its scent into every pore, into his nose and down his throat, as the tired tailor dragged and carried three poor souls to the garden. He would dig one grave only — there was no time or strength for more. Wild dogs and foxes and badgers and many more dangerous beasts, among them wolves and bears would creep out at this hour to explore nature’s larder. The tailor would have to work quickly as the night rose. Better those animals fed in the garden than there inside the tavern.

The tailor found a garden fork in the stable. He then rolled up his sleeves and relit the lantern. Its flickering light danced over the pile of bodies. The soil was cold and stubborn. Each shovel of earth felt heavier than the last.

A twig snapped somewhere behind him. He froze. The woods held their breath. A single pair of eyes blinked from the treeline — low, patient, watching.

He dug faster, breath ragged, sweat chilling on his neck. When the grave was finally covered, the eyes vanished into the undergrowth.

Then, the tailor crept back inside the shelter of the tavern and barred the windows and doors. He shivered as he poured a large tumbler of whisky. The tailor swigged it down, tears and all. The drink burnt the fear away. Having no barman to pay, the tailor was generous, and helped himself to a second dram.

He gathered some wood, lit a roaring fire and fell — sat in an armchair, holding the garden fork in one hand, and a third, very generous glass of whisky in the other. He was ready for anything and everything that might try to come through the door. A sleepless night awaited him.

Daylight soon came. A travelling priest knocked on the door, then pushed down on the iron latch. The priest took a step back, not daring to believe the vision that he found before him. A husk of a man in the chair, withered and dry, his life seemingly sucked away. His face was full of fear and sorrow, and the lines on his face were etched as if doused in acid. A filthy garden fork was lying on the floor, and an empty glass had rolled through the dust.

The priest eyeballed the whole tavern. Smoke smouldered in the fireplace. He saw one corpse first — hanging alone, gently swaying. Then, as he stepped further in, the second corpse revealed itself in the dimmer rafters, its legs drifting as if stirred by a breath that did not exist.

A cautious and penitent man, the priest stepped in and heaved the door shut. He wondered why it was so heavy, and that’s when he saw the smiling dead man pinned to the door. Was this real? It was real enough for him to flee.

He had found a tavern for the dead. Stumbling in fear, blood pumping in his temples, the priest turned and ran, and ran, and ran, until his very soul turned white with fear. The faint sound of his body, dropping dead into the hidden undergrowth wafted through the silent woods. His corpse was grabbed by the roots below, for the tavern was a monster that lived off the unfortunate visitors that came from far and wide.

item.title: Archipelago
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Homo species

Huddled around the dancing tongues they watched the scarlet horizon stretch and disappear, pinpricked stars twinkled through a velvet draped vista, skeletal trees and plants seemingly absorbed by the quicksand of the black swampy night.

Once the fire was roaring, communication began. The pelt-clad people communicated to those near, those far, those alive and those past. Rituals helped pass information to the young. A handful of young of the right age sparkled around the fire like embers on the thermals, the long childhood gave time for speech and learning.

The day had been successful and the gatherers had brown nuts, swollen ripe fruits and berries in their simple woven grass baskets. Crimson pools domed, the deer carcasses hung from wooden struts held together by woven strips of tree bark, the beginnings of a basic rope. Some hung the deer head to the sky, some hooves to the sky. Hooves to the sky and the blood would drain, head to the sky to remove the intestines and internal organs, avoiding them falling into the chest cavity.

The elders showed the young both methods, how to use a flint and bones to scrape the hide, and then watched as the young practiced. They knew the environment and its dangers. Not specialists but flexible and adaptable, the Elders made sure that roots, plants and leaves were recognised so that no accidents occurred. They also knew where to find honey and how to weave fish traps .

The Elders also communicated with the plants and animals, the wind and the rain,the seasons and the dead. They knew that soon there would be babies, and the power to speak to the spirits would be granted to one, and the power to communicate through thought over great distances would be granted to another. These things were know through dances and drumbeats, and reputation. One female, Young Lake had been seen in their visions.

The elders had gathered around a fire and then danced. Special offerings and herbs were burnt and then the elders had gone to the biggest hut, the one paved inside and covered with the most skins covering the branches on the outside. All ten elders ate the special mushrooms, and sat in a trance. Their visions would lead the clan for the upcoming seasons. Young Lake would bear one of the special young, but the other was bounded in clouded mystery.

The females led the young to the hidden caves, with the trembling stone lamp brim full of burning animal fat, the paintings showing water, routes, others, prey, and abstract symbols with a specific meaning. The walls seemed to flicker and dance, preparing the youth to face large pray but also to read the symbols, to survive.

Dance and song echoed in the caves, the sacred rituals and marks, the passage to the sacred spaces. Footfall was muffled by the pelts and dried vegetation that covered most of the entrance of the cave. It was here that the women gave birth, in the shelter of the cave but near the entrance, protected from the elements and close to the fire. The group knew that only few children would survive , and even the pregnant females risked a messy death. More than half the clan were children. Playful children would break an arm or fall, get injured. Injured children lagged behind and were picked off by preditors.

Or their wounds would get infected, or they got infections from their milk teeth falling out and their infected gums would kill them. Or childhood diseases or bacteria would kill whole clans. The elders knew some plants could help with illnesses but also that many children would die before 5, from parasites, or diarrhoea, or infectious diseases like tuberculosis. There was no long childhood however and once puberty hit at around eight years old , most dangers would be removed, except predation.

Pictures seemed to dance across the cave face. Daubed by the clan, they hid animals, communication, pathways, waterways, food and other information. The clan was cyclically nomadic, staying put in places for a few months and then moved on. They built primitive benders, shelters of bent tree branches and covered by hides or leaves, with more hides on the floors, and even in the larger ones flat stones would be covered by pelts to soften the footfall.

Weaving the shelters together was done by song, to teach others. The tribe members also wove sticks together to make small baskets to carry things. All the clan taught the children the songs, the marks , the movements.

Over time, meeting with the Others had become less risky. Before Blue Jay, the young female was born, eight years ago, the clan had met the Others for the first time. It ahd been violent, bad tempered at first, but after the first fears, things settled; The others would give the clan some youngsters in exchange for some of the clan’s, and tools, knowledge, food and even a meal would be shared. But the meetings didn’t last long. Too many people in one place woàuld cause animalks to visit, and tempers to flair. Three moons was enough, as food would run out, or people would run out of patience. The Others hunted bigger animals, and were stro,nger so there was no ,point trying to fight them. A visit had to be fleeting a,nd of mutual interest.

They crouched close to the fire as the last red seam of sun sank behind the trees. Smoke braided upward and vanished into the thickening dark. One by one, stars pierced the sky. Beyond the ring of light the swamp swallowed shape and distance; tree trunks thinned to bone and dissolved.

When the flames steadied, voices rose.

Not speeches—bursts of sound, hands cutting the air, shoulders hunched and lifted. A hunter mimed the stagger of the deer; another snapped a twig and the children flinched, then laughed. An old woman leaned forward and drew a line in ash with a charred stick: river, bend, crossing. A boy reached to smudge it and she caught his wrist, squeezing once before letting go. Watch.

The gatherers tipped their woven grass baskets onto hides. Brown nuts rattled. Split figs bled syrup. Berries rolled like beads into waiting hands. Nearby, two deer hung from a wooden frame lashed with twisted bark. One carcass dangled head-down, dark blood dripping into a shallow scrape in the soil. The other hung by its hind legs; a man slit the belly carefully, easing the organs free so they would not spill back into the chest. Steam rose in the cooling air.

A girl knelt with a flake of flint and scraped hide from flesh. Her strokes were clumsy at first. An elder shifted her grip without a word, guiding her wrist until the blade found its rhythm. Beside them, someone worried sinew from a leg, rolling it against his thigh to make cord.

They did not divide the world into teachers and students. Knowledge passed hand to hand: which roots snapped clean and which bled white poison; which leaves soothed a sting; where bees nested in the hollow trees upriver; how stones, set just so, funneled fish into waiting baskets when the water fell.

Later, when the moon lifted pale and thin, a different quiet settled.

In the largest shelter—branches bent and tied, hides layered thick against the wind—several of the oldest sat close together. The air smelled of crushed leaves and something bitter burning in the coals. They swayed, eyes half-lidded, listening to the drumbeat thudded softly on stretched skin. Breath slowed. Shoulders loosened. In the morning they would speak of what they had seen: the herds turning early, the river rising fast, a child standing alone on a ridge. Patterns, not certainties. The band would weigh their words.

Young Lake sat near the entrance, fingers pressed to her abdomen. The old women watched her when they thought she did not notice.

At the caves, the children carried stone lamps cupped in both hands, fat wicks trembling. Light leapt across the walls and the painted animals seemed to move—bison lowering their heads, red deer stepping from shadow, handprints blooming and fading with the flicker. The women sang low, guiding the young along the narrow passage, showing them where the river bent, where cliffs broke, where strangers had once appeared out of the trees. Marks layered over marks. Memory held in ochre and charcoal.

Near the cave mouth, where air still moved and smoke could escape, a space lay cleared. Pelts softened the stone. Here women labored, gripping hands, biting leather, voices rising and falling with the contractions. Blood darkened the ground. Sometimes a newborn’s cry cut sharp and strong through the night. Sometimes it did not.

More than half the band were children. They tumbled over one another in play, chasing sparks, wrestling in leaves. A broken arm meant careful splinting with bark and hope. A deep cut meant watching for the heat and swelling that could follow. Some fevers burned out; some did not. Loose bowels could empty a small body in days. A cough might linger all winter. They knew plants that eased pain, leaves that slowed bleeding, clays that dried a wound—but they also knew the stillness that sometimes came despite all of it.

Childhood stretched long. Limbs lengthened slowly. Voices thickened years after the first hunt with a real spear. Only when hair roughened at the jaw and hips widened did new dangers replace the old.

Their shelters were bent saplings anchored in the earth, lashed with cord and roofed with hides and brush. Stones lined the hearths. Inside, the ground was layered with grass and skins. They stayed until the nearby stands thinned and the traps came up empty, until the river shifted or the wind changed its bite. Then they lifted what they could carry and followed remembered paths.

Songs stitched the work together—how to set the poles, how to twist fiber, how to shape a point. Every child learned the verses because every child would need them.

They had not always met the Others.

Years ago, before Blue Jay was born, shapes had appeared across the river—taller figures, heavier spears, unfamiliar calls. The first meeting had been a scatter of shouts and thrown stones. No one slept that night.

But hunger travels farther than fear. Later, at the edge of a clearing, they approached again. Gifts were set down and hands lifted empty. A flint blade changed owners. So did a necklace of teeth. They shared meat once, crouched in a wide circle, eyes never quite leaving one another.

Too many bodies in one place drew scavengers. Voices sharpened. After a handful of nights the Others drifted away, taking with them a young man who had been watching their toolmaker too closely, leaving behind a girl who did not look back.

Three moons was long enough.

Beyond the firelight, something moved in the reeds. The band tightened its circle. A child leaned into an elder’s side. The elder fed another branch to the flames and watched the sparks climb, measuring the dark.

Now it was time again Exchanges would be made, knowledge shared. At the highest sun they would leave, with new young , new goods and new knowledge.

Nomads made some innovations, the ones that were portable and that went with the herds they followed. They would have to live off the roots and plants as well as the carrion they found along the way, Things explained by clan members in flittering nights

Meeting the Others was always as close to, the highest sun as possible. It made it safer to travel and the days lasted longer, or at least daylight did.

Around the embers of the fire, gestures and chewing showed how to make cord, hide, stone tools.

Migration meant only light tools could be carried, or that tools would be made on the way.

Yellow Flower, and River Rushes were two females, aged about eight years old. Together with Blue Jay they ran and played, tugging at each other’s hair, the elder women watched. They knew Blue jay had felt this strange feeling for some moons now. Yellow Flower and River Rushes perhaps too. That night they took the three aside. Blue Jay felt the wetness of blood flowing on her legs. The elders had collected some wild flowers and placed them in Blue jays hair. They took Yellow Flower and River Rushes to see.

Blue Jay was standing in the glade, naked. They saw the blood, the elder women showed them. River Rushes and Yellow Flower thought it was an injury, blood was a bad sign. But this was a good sign. Another woman , older, stood next to Blue Jay. She too stripped, her breasts in the moon light. She too had blood.

The women used gestures to explain. This bleeding would happen sometimes, but not always. It lasted a few days, and not much blood was lost. Changes to their bodies, the breasts, and hips came. Males would see you differently. The time of play had ended.

They came back to the clan’s resting place, each girl had a flower in her hair. It was a sign to the others, the menarch had started. Not old enough to breed yet, but not a girl any more.

The Others

Lionel

Lionel moved through the village the way a man moves through a room he built himself — not looking, exactly, because he no longer needed to look. His face still held the softness of youth, though he was the oldest man on the island. Sun and salt had done that carving, not years.

He'd been thirteen, maybe fourteen, when the Shamans took him under the twenty-first full moon and looked at him with their clouded eyes until he understood something had already been decided.

Five children this year. He walked them to the rock pools at low tide, watched one crouch motionless for an hour waiting on a crab, watched another chase a shrimp too fast to ever catch. He didn't tell them what he saw. He never did. The Shamans would ask him later, and he would answer, and that was the whole of his teaching: watching, then naming what he'd watched.

The island spoke in spears. One planted outside a hut: stay out. Three set in a tripod by the long hut: safe. Two gaps in that tripod: another tribe was coming. Three gaps: nature had turned dangerous. Four: war.

That evening the gaps meant nothing he'd taught the children to read.

He was sitting near the gathering place when the rock pools clouded — not with the tide, but from underneath, sediment rising the way blood rises in water. Then a burst of fish, colours too bright for the hour, gone before he could be sure he'd seen them. The pool went still after. Too still. It held the first stars like a held breath.

The elders lit fires they hadn't planned to light. Spears went up in the two-gap warning before anyone had agreed there was anything to warn about. A chicken's throat was opened over the threshold of the long hut, and its feathers went into the fire, and the smell of that stayed in Lionel's throat longer than it should have.

He went out alone and gathered palm leaves and held them over embers until they curled. He said the words his teacher had said before him — not because he believed the words did anything, but because his hands needed the shape of the ritual to keep from shaking. He opened the coco stone. Five Shamans, five portions, Five children ; the smallest measure kept for the worst nights.

He knelt and drew lines in the dirt with one finger.

"We walk the maze tomorrow," he said. "The signs won't untangle themselves standing still."

By morning he'd salted the undergrowth against anything that might use the confusion to hunt, and they went in formation, spears out, until the trees opened onto the mud pool.

It was breathing wrong. Bubbles came up in bursts instead of the slow roll he knew, and each burst threw steam that smelled faintly of struck flint. He crouched at the edge and watched a shape move under the surface — not an animal's shape, not quite — and the men closed the circle tighter around him, spears turned outward like quills.

Mist came off the trees and swallowed the colour first, then the sound. Something crossed the edge of his sight and was gone before he could turn his head to it. He held still. He had learned, before he had learned almost anything else, that stillness was the only offering the island ever asked for.

Then the mist thinned on its own, the way it always eventually did, and the shapes went with it, and the danger — whatever it had been — passed the way weather passes.

The moon came up clean.

Lionel stood at the edge of the pool a long while after the others had turned back toward the fires. He had read the signs. He had done everything the reading required. And still he did not know what any of it meant — only that the island had troubled itself to speak, and that a man could spend his whole life being fluent in a language and still not know, on the night it mattered most, what he'd just been told.

He woke and headed to the village. He knew the villages half dreaded, half praised his visit. Another tribe was coming, it had been seen. He had time to select 5 children and train them, only just, before they came. A trade would happen, or a child would decide to stay.

item.title: Laura’s Thread
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Laura’s Thread —
Laura had discovered knitting by accident. One rainy afternoon she wandered into the local craft store, drawn by the warm light and the soft colours stacked on the shelves. The women inside welcomed her instantly, guiding her hands through the first clumsy stitches. Soon she was visiting every week, buying yarns she didn’t need, bobbins she didn’t understand, and needles in every size. Knitting became her refuge — a quiet, repetitive rhythm that drowned out the noise of her life.Her marriage had been unraveling for years. Her husband drifted from job to job, always tired, always complaining, always collapsing onto the sofa with the weight of a man who expected the world to carry him. Laura had carried him. She had carried him far too long.The betrayal with her sister had been the final tear. She had discovered it in a way that felt almost staged: a message left open, a glance exchanged, a silence too heavy to ignore. Her sister had not denied it. Her husband had barely apologised. Laura had not spoken to her sister since.

Now they were all travelling together — her husband, her sister, her new partner Kathy, and Laura herself — on a three‑hour drive to La Rochelle to visit her grandmother. Laura sat in the back seat, knitting the first jumper she had ever attempted. The yarn was soft, pale blue, the colour of calm seas. She made sure her seatbelt was firmly clicked in. She didn’t trust her husband’s driving, and she trusted her sister even less.

But Laura had prepared for this trip.A week earlier, she had noticed the car door seals were worn. She patched them quietly, carefully, making sure no one saw. She siphoned off the brake fluid and stored it in the house, telling herself it was temporary, telling herself she was only being cautious. She knew about the odour it left behind. She poured the brake fluid into the back of the car just before they left, her hands steady, her breath calm.She told herself she wasn’t planning anything. She told herself she was only thinking.The motorway stretched ahead in a long grey ribbon. Her husband talked loudly, gesturing at nothing. Her sister laughed at something

Kathy whispered. Laura kept knitting, the needles clicking softly, a heartbeat she controlled.Then the lorry in front of them braked.Her husband reacted too slowly.

He had been talking, distracted. The car slammed forward, metal folding like cloth. Laura felt her knitting needles jerk in her hands; she grabbed the gear lever as the impact threw her forward. The seat in front of her pierced her husband’s side. Time slowed, then collapsed into silence.Emergency services arrived. They cut them from the wreckage. Laura drifted in and out of consciousness, the world a blur of lights and voices.She woke in a hospital room, surrounded by friends and family. The doctors told her she had been lucky. Her husband and her sister had not survived.The police visited her soon after. A woman officer asked gentle questions. Laura could barely remember anything. The officer mentioned the knitting needles — how they had gone straight through the car seat behind her. Laura shivered. The officer reassured her that she wasn’t responsible, that she should focus on healing.But Laura remembered the brake fluid.
She remembered the patched seals.
She remembered the odour.She cried for a long time after the police left.In the quiet of the hospital room, she stared at the ceiling. The red glow of the emergency exit sign painted the walls in a strange, warm hue. She remembered losing the sharp needles. She remembered her husband’s voice telling her once, half‑joking, that she’d kill him someday with her “ridiculous hobbies.”Knitting wasn’t just for grandmothers. It was an innocent habit, a craft she had cultivated carefully. And now, with the insurance payout and the sudden quiet of her life, she realised she had crafted something else entirely: a future without the people who had betrayed her.But the story didn’t end there.A week after she returned home, Laura found a letter slipped under her door. No stamp. No name. Just a single sentence written in a familiar hand:“You didn’t think I’d leave you alone, did you?”Her sister’s handwriting.Laura stared at the letter, her breath tightening.
She had seen her sister’s body.
She had attended the funeral.
She had watched the coffin lower into the earth.Yet the handwriting was unmistakable.The next day, a second letter arrived.
Then a third.

Each one more unsettling than the last.Someone knew what she had done.
Someone knew about the brake fluid.
Someone knew about the patched seals.And someone was coming.Laura picked up her knitting needles — the new pair she had bought after the accident. The metal glinted in the lamplight. Her hands were steady.

She had crafted her freedom once.She could do it again.

item.title: Ages for Agnes
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
Agnes’s life never moved in straight lines; it unfolded like a coastline, bending and curving with storms and quiet tides. She remembered the first time she stood on a ship’s deck at twenty, boots too big, hair dyed jet‑black to look older. The wind slapped her cheeks, sharp and cold, and she tasted salt on her lips. The chief officer barked at her to keep her eyes forward. She didn’t bother to answer. She already was.

The sea taught her its language: the groan of ropes under strain, the metallic thrum of engines, the way the air changed seconds before a storm. She learned to read clouds like maps and silence like warning. She slept in a narrow bunk that smelled of diesel and damp wool, and woke each morning with the sense that she was becoming someone she hadn’t yet met.

By forty, she was captain. Her boots thudded across the deck with authority, and crew members straightened when she passed. Her hair was still black then, tied tight, a symbol of command. She could smell storms before the instruments detected them — a metallic tang, a sudden drop in temperature, the horizon bruising purple.

“Captain, storm ahead,” someone would call. “I know,” she’d reply. “I can smell it.”

Her cabin smelled of coffee and old maps. She had lovers in ports, friends in harbours, and a reputation that travelled faster than the wind. But she also had a letter from home she never opened, tucked in the drawer beneath her charts.

When she finally returned at fifty, the funeral home smelled of lilies and dust. Her brother hugged her tightly, surprised she’d come back at all. Silver threaded through her hair now, soft and honest. She touched the cracked tiles of the old building, feeling the texture of neglect.

“This place needs a captain,” she said.

And she became one.

She rebuilt the business the way she’d once steered ships through storms — with precision, stubbornness, and a refusal to accept anything less than excellence. She stood among builders, pointing, correcting, commanding. When a beam sat crooked, she tapped it with her boot.

“You call that level?” The foreman laughed nervously. “Captain’s orders, then.” “Captain’s orders.”

She installed computers before anyone else dared. She brought in the internet. She created a post‑box system that filled funerals with mourners again. Her days smelled of printer ink and fresh paint; her nights tasted of exhaustion and quiet pride.

By sixty‑five, she was travelling again — not across oceans, but across regions. Rain‑soaked train platforms, warm handshakes, care‑home directors offering tea. Her silver hair became her signature. Her dark humour became legend.

“Grey Acid,” they called her. She didn’t mind. She liked watching people laugh at jokes they shouldn’t.

Her colleagues adored her. Her clients trusted her. Her friends knew she carried storms inside her still.

At eighty, the farewell began. Champagne fizzed in tall glasses. The room buzzed with voices, laughter, memories. Bernadette spotted her first and pulled her into a hug.

“You’re glowing.” “I’m eighty,” Agnes replied. “I’m not glowing. I’m reflecting.”

Laughter rippled through the room. Someone shouted, “The old bitch does have a heart!” Agnes raised her glass. “Don’t spread it around.”

Martin approached, eyes misty. “You taught me how to talk to grieving families.” Agnes squeezed his shoulder. “I taught you to listen. That’s different.”

Elise handed her a brass compass. “You always find your way.” Agnes closed the lid gently. “Not always.”

Later, alone in her office, she wrote notes to every client contact. Her handwriting was slow but steady. When she finished, she leaned back and exhaled.

“That’s it,” she whispered. “Done.”

Her new home near the lake smelled of lemon polish and cooling tea. The water outside hummed with insects and the soft lap of waves against stone. She walked through the park of remembrance, breathing in damp leaves and pine. Cornflowers bloomed along the path, blue against dark soil. A child traced names on a memorial stone. A man fed birds near the fountain. Agnes watched them, feeling decades shift inside her — not heavy, but present.

That evening, Bernadette arrived with whisky.

“You didn’t think I’d let you spend your first night alone, did you?” Agnes smirked. “I was hoping.”

They drank. They laughed. They remembered.

“You ever regret leaving the sea?” Bernadette asked. Agnes considered. “No. I regret not leaving sooner.”

“You always were impossible.”

Agnes leaned back, letting the quiet fill the room. “I built something good,” she said. “Something that mattered.” “You did,” Bernadette replied. “And you didn’t do it alone.” “No,” Agnes said softly. “I didn’t.”

Later, after Bernadette left, Agnes lit candles. The flame flickered like a heartbeat. She touched photographs — lovers, friends, children, storms, ships, branches, clients, decades.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

For the first time in her life, she had nowhere to be in the morning. No clients. No branches. No storms.

Just the lake. Just the silver hair. Just the long, earned peace.

And somewhere in that peace, a spark flickered — not duty, not obligation, but possibility.

She smiled.

“Maybe,” she said softly, “I’m not done yet.”

item.title: Measuring Culture
item.dc:creator: idreamofthought
item.content:encoded:
1. What culture is and why it exists

Culture is not a measure of superiority or advancement. It arises naturally from human activities, exchanges, and interactions. Many elements of culture — art, music, symbols, rituals — go back tens of thousands of years. Cave art, petroglyphs, counting marks on bones, burials, and early rituals all show that humans (and even Neanderthals) created cultural expressions long before writing existed.

2. Prehistoric foundations of culture

Archaeological evidence shows:

  • Cave art as early as 70,000 BCE (Blombos Cave)
  • Cave paintings around 45,500 years ago
  • Neanderthal musical instruments around 60,000 years ago
  • Paleolithic flutes around 35,000 years ago

From these early practices emerged ideas that shaped humanity: language, mathematics, religion, symbolism, and storytelling.

Compare that to writing, or even numbers. The earliest finds we have showing that people were probably counting are things like the Ishango Bone, (from around 20 thousand years ago but debated) or the much older Lebombo bone, from around 40 thousand years ago, but debated) and tally marks on cave walls. Culture predates all of this.

3. Culture as local and global

Cultural practices could be local or widespread. Cave art, burial rituals, and trade networks appear across the world. Some practices were adopted, others abandoned, and many changed due to:

  • invasions
  • migrations
  • climate shifts
  • technological improvements

Shared styles may explain similarities between sites thousands of years old, though we cannot assume a single cultural thread linking them all.

4. Geography, movement, and cultural exchange

Culture continually shifts. Trade by river, sea, or land routes spread ideas and habits. Geographical barriers — mountains, seas, valleys — created isolation, distinct languages, and unique cultural traits. Technological improvements in sailing and transport increased cultural exchange.

Today, the internet accelerates cultural change daily, making culture more fluid than ever.

5. Understanding other cultures — and stereotypes

We only truly know the cultures we are exposed to. When encountering unfamiliar cultures, they may seem strange, frightening, or incomprehensible. This often leads to mockery or stereotypes.

Examples:

  • French people “mock” English eating habits.
  • English people “mock” French eating habits.

Yet stereotypes rarely match reality: few French people eat snails or frogs daily, and English roast beef is no longer a universal Sunday tradition.

6. Culture in personal experience

Even within one lifetime, culture changes. Practices once common become rare; traditions fade or transform. What was taboo becomes accepted or even normal. Society still maintains social and legal norms, but expectations evolve rapidly.

7. Religion as an example of cultural change

In the UK, religious identity has shifted dramatically:

  • In 1983: 66% Christian, 31% no religion
  • In 2018: 38% Christian, 52% non‑religious

Church attendance has fallen by hundreds of thousands. Where most people once attended church weekly, now most do not.

8. Cultural traces that remain

Despite change, culture leaves marks everywhere:

  • French day names come from Roman gods.
  • English day names come from Viking gods.
  • Christianity adapted earlier Celtic festivals.
  • Words like Friday (Frigg/Frija) and Easter (possibly Eostre) preserve ancient mythologies.

9. The difficulty of defining culture

Culture is vast, shifting, and complex. As soon as we try to measure or capture it, it changes. We stand in the present, looking back at what was lost, what survived, and what transformed — like King Canute trying to command the tide.

Some have tried to measure culture, Geerte Hofstede, Erin Meyers among others. but even their attempts needed updates and are probably outdated even now.
